challenges.title: AI and machine learning
challenges.description: Which statement describes the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)?

choices.text: ML is one approach within the broader field of AI.
AI is one approach within the broader field of ML.
AI and ML are names for the same algorithm.
All AI systems learn from examples.

challenges.hint: Think of the wider field and one way to build its systems.

solution.code: ML is one approach within the broader field of AI.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: AI covers a broad range of approaches to intelligent tasks; ML learns patterns from data.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: An AI system can also use explicitly written rules, so not all AI is ML.

challenges.title: Recognizing structured data
challenges.description: Which example is structured data?

choices.text: A set of free-form customer emails.
A table with one row per order and fixed date, item, and price columns.
A folder of customer voicemail recordings.
A collection of product photographs.

challenges.hint: Look for a consistent schema of named fields.

solution.code: A table with one row per order and fixed date, item, and price columns.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The order table uses the same named columns for every row.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Audio, photos, and free-form text do not themselves have that tabular structure.

challenges.title: Rows in a dataset
challenges.description: A dataset for predicting house prices has one row per house. What does one row represent?

choices.text: A rule that the model has learned.
A measure of the model's accuracy.
One example: a house and its recorded values.
The entire collection of houses.

challenges.hint: Identify the individual item the data describes.

solution.code: One example: a house and its recorded values.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Each row describes one house, with values such as area and sale price.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The dataset is the collection of all those rows, not a single row.

challenges.title: A weighted prediction
challenges.description: A simple model predicts a value as 2 × x + 3. What does it predict when x is 4?
challenges.hint: Multiply the input by its weight, then add the constant.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: First calculate 2 × 4 = 8; then add 3 to get 11.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The constant is added after multiplication; it is not multiplied by x.

challenges.title: An unusually large value
challenges.description: The values are 2, 3, 4, and 31. What happens to their mean if 31 is removed?

choices.text: It decreases.
It increases.
It stays the same.
It becomes the largest remaining value.

challenges.hint: Compare the unusually large value with the rest.

solution.code: It decreases.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The mean is 10 with all four values and 3 without 31.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A large outlier can pull the mean upward.

challenges.title: Choosing a plot
challenges.description: You want to see how customer ages are distributed across ranges. Which plot is most directly suited to this?

choices.text: A table of customer names.
A histogram of customer ages.
A scatter plot of age against income.
A line plot of one customer's age over time.

challenges.hint: You need counts within ranges of a single numeric variable.

solution.code: A histogram of customer ages.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: A histogram groups ages into bins and shows how many observations fall in each.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A scatter plot is more useful for inspecting the relationship between two variables.

challenges.title: Inspecting data
challenges.description: Before training on a table, which check can reveal incomplete input records?

choices.text: Increase the model's learning rate.
Sort the model's predictions by confidence.
Count missing values in each column.
Measure the model's final test accuracy.

challenges.hint: Look for absent values before a model is trained.

solution.code: Count missing values in each column.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Counting null or missing values shows which columns have incomplete records.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Model accuracy and prediction confidence are not available until a model has been evaluated.

challenges.title: A prediction and an outcome
challenges.description: A model estimates tomorrow's sales as 120 units. What is 120?

choices.text: The observed sales for tomorrow.
A feature used to train every model.
Proof that the model is accurate.
The model's prediction for tomorrow.

challenges.hint: The estimate is made before the actual sales are known.

solution.code: The model's prediction for tomorrow.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The model output is an estimate of a future outcome.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Accuracy can only be assessed by comparing predictions with observed outcomes.

challenges.title: Learning from labeled examples
challenges.description: A dataset contains emails labeled spam or not spam. Training a model to predict those labels is which kind of learning?

choices.text: Supervised learning.
Unsupervised clustering.
Manual data entry.
Dimensionality reduction without labels.

challenges.hint: The examples include the desired output.

solution.code: Supervised learning.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Supervised learning uses examples paired with target labels.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Clustering groups examples without requiring a target label for each one.

challenges.title: House-price inputs
challenges.description: A model predicts a house's eventual sale price using its floor area at listing time. Which is the label?

choices.text: The list of all house records.
The eventual sale price.
The floor area.
The model's training algorithm.

challenges.hint: The label is the outcome the model is trained to predict.

solution.code: The eventual sale price.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Sale price is the target value in each labeled training example.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Floor area is an input feature available when the prediction is made.

challenges.title: Consistent date formats
challenges.description: A date column contains both '2025-03-08' and '03/08/2025'. What is a sensible cleaning step if the second format is documented as month/day/year?

choices.text: Replace every date with today's date.
Delete the entire dataset.
Parse both formats and store dates consistently.
Treat both dates as missing regardless of their meaning.

challenges.hint: Use the known format to interpret each value before standardizing it.

solution.code: Parse both formats and store dates consistently.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Both strings can be parsed as the same date and represented consistently.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Without the documented format, the second string could be ambiguous and would need clarification.

challenges.title: Class or number?
challenges.description: A model must decide whether an incoming email is spam or not spam. What type of prediction is this?

choices.text: Regression of a continuous quantity.
Forecasting a numerical time series.
Calculating a dataset's mean.
Binary classification.

challenges.hint: The required output is one of two categories.

solution.code: Binary classification.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Spam and not spam are two discrete classes.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Regression instead predicts a numeric quantity such as a price.

challenges.title: Predicting a price
challenges.description: A model estimates a house's sale price in dollars. Which task is this?

choices.text: Regression.
Binary classification.
Clustering without a target.
Counting missing values.

challenges.hint: The target is a numeric amount rather than a category.

solution.code: Regression.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Regression estimates a numerical target such as sale price.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The model can be evaluated by measuring the difference between estimated and actual prices.

challenges.title: A held-out evaluation
challenges.description: After defining a prediction problem and preparing data, what should you do before deploying a trained model?

choices.text: Skip evaluation if training completed without errors.
Evaluate it on data held out from training.
Declare it accurate because it fitted the training data.
Use the final test outcomes as input features.

challenges.hint: Check how well the model performs on examples it did not learn from.

solution.code: Evaluate it on data held out from training.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: A held-out evaluation provides evidence about performance on unseen examples.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Training performance alone cannot establish that the model generalizes.

challenges.title: Matching a use case
challenges.description: A store wants to suggest products to shoppers based on their past interactions. Which AI use case fits this goal?

choices.text: Formatting a spreadsheet.
Calculating a dataset's row count.
Recommendation.
Measuring missing values.

challenges.hint: The system must select items a person may find relevant.

solution.code: Recommendation.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: A recommender ranks or selects products for a shopper.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Data cleaning and counting may support the work, but neither directly provides recommendations.

challenges.title: Choosing rules or learning
challenges.description: A thermostat must heat a room whenever it is below 18 degrees C. The requirement is fixed and explicit. Which approach is the clearest start?

choices.text: Write a direct temperature rule.
Train a model to discover the threshold from examples.
Cluster rooms by temperature.
Predict tomorrow's outdoor temperature.

challenges.hint: Notice whether the desired behavior is already stated precisely.

solution.code: Write a direct temperature rule.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The requirement gives an exact condition and action; it need not be inferred from examples.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A direct rule is inspectable and avoids unnecessary learning for stable behavior.

challenges.title: When machine learning helps
challenges.description: A shop cannot write simple rules for which products a customer may want, but has many examples of browsing and purchases. Why might ML help?

choices.text: It guarantees every suggestion is correct.
It removes the need to define useful suggestions.
It can learn recurring patterns from those examples.
It turns every purchase into a hand-written rule.

challenges.hint: Consider what the examples provide that a fixed rule list lacks.

solution.code: It can learn recurring patterns from those examples.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Past interactions can reveal relationships between behavior and later choices.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Learned patterns can help with suggestions but cannot guarantee correctness or define success.

challenges.title: Mixed Table Text
challenges.description: A sales table has regular date, store, and amount columns, plus a review field containing free-form paragraphs. How should the data be described?

choices.text: The entire dataset is unstructured because one column is text.
The table has a structured layout, while the review values are unstructured text.
The review paragraphs are numeric labels.
Every field is a fixed category because it is in a table.

challenges.hint: Distinguish the table's organization from the contents of an individual field.

solution.code: The table has a structured layout, while the review values are unstructured text.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The rows and columns form a consistent schema, but review paragraphs do not follow a fixed set of fields.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A table can combine structured columns with text that needs its own processing.

challenges.title: Email data format
challenges.description: A company stores messages as free-form email text. Before a model expecting numeric columns can use them, what is a sensible step?

choices.text: Treat each entire email as a numeric label.
Assume the subject is always the answer.
Delete all text because only tables are useful.
Represent or extract useful information from the text.

challenges.hint: Ask what input form the model expects and what form the email has.

solution.code: Represent or extract useful information from the text.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Free-form text needs processing into a representation the chosen model accepts.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Text can be useful, but it is not automatically a numeric feature table or target.

challenges.title: Understanding data types
challenges.description: Two files both end in .csv. One contains consistent measurement columns; the other has one column of paragraphs. What should you inspect to understand their structure?

choices.text: Only the file extension.
The computer used to save them.
The schema and how values are represented.
The filename length.

challenges.hint: A suffix may not describe the meaning of contents.

solution.code: The schema and how values are represented.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Columns and representations show whether values are tabular measurements or unstructured text.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The same extension can contain different content; the suffix alone is not enough.

challenges.title: Dataset Region Coverage
challenges.description: A team trains a delivery model using records only from the downtown area, then plans to use it across the whole city. What should it check?

choices.text: Whether the examples represent conditions in the other neighborhoods too.
Whether downtown records have the shortest row numbers.
Whether the model can memorize every downtown address.
Whether the dataset has a column named city.

challenges.hint: Compare where examples came from with where the model will be used.

solution.code: Whether the examples represent conditions in the other neighborhoods too.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A downtown-only sample may miss patterns in neighborhoods with different roads or traffic.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A suitable dataset should reflect the intended population; a city column or memorization cannot ensure that.

challenges.title: Verified Target Labels
challenges.description: A training set uses last year's model guesses as the labels for new cases, without checking actual outcomes. What is the main risk?

choices.text: The examples automatically become verified ground truth.
The input features disappear when labels are copied.
The model can no longer make predictions.
The new model may learn to repeat the old model's mistakes.

challenges.hint: Ask whether the labels are observed outcomes or another model's estimates.

solution.code: The new model may learn to repeat the old model's mistakes.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Unverified predictions do not establish what actually happened in each case.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Training on those guesses can reproduce their errors instead of learning the intended target.

challenges.title: Seasonal Data Coverage
challenges.description: A store trains a demand model using only summer sales but plans to use it throughout the year. What is an important data concern?

choices.text: Summer records cannot contain numeric features.
Winter examples may have different patterns that the data does not represent.
The model will always predict zero in winter.
The calendar date must be the target label.

challenges.hint: Consider whether every season is represented in examples for year-round use.

solution.code: Winter examples may have different patterns that the data does not represent.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Sales patterns may vary by season, so summer-only data may not capture winter behavior.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The gap is a representativeness concern, not proof of a particular prediction or a change to the target.

challenges.title: Grouping Repeat Customer Records
challenges.description: A dataset has multiple orders per shopper. If rows are split randomly, orders from one shopper may appear in both training and evaluation. What is the concern?

choices.text: The evaluation may not represent performance on shoppers the model has never seen.
The model will lose all order amounts.
Every shopper will become a target label.
Random splitting guarantees the groups are independent.

challenges.hint: Notice that rows from the same person can be related to one another.

solution.code: The evaluation may not represent performance on shoppers the model has never seen.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The model may recognize shopper-specific patterns in evaluation rows already represented during training.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Keeping each shopper's records together when splitting can better test use on new shoppers.

challenges.title: Reading a feature vector
challenges.description: For one house, a model receives [2, 85, 1998], meaning bedrooms, floor area, and build year. What does each number represent?

choices.text: A separate house-price prediction.
A model accuracy score.
A value for one of the house's input features.
One of three possible house labels.

challenges.hint: Use the stated order of features to interpret entries.

solution.code: A value for one of the house's input features.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Each position holds one numeric feature value for that house.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The vector describes inputs, not multiple outputs, evaluation, or alternative labels.

challenges.title: Aligning Features And Weights
challenges.description: A simple score uses 2 times temperature plus 5 times humidity. The input list is reordered from [temperature, humidity] to [humidity, temperature]. What must also change?

choices.text: The score must be replaced with a class label.
The corresponding weights must be reordered to stay matched with each feature.
Both inputs must be changed to dates.
No change is needed because weights always apply to every input equally.

challenges.hint: Each coefficient belongs to a particular input, not just a position-free list.

solution.code: The corresponding weights must be reordered to stay matched with each feature.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The first weight was for temperature and the second for humidity.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Reordering inputs without their matching weights changes the calculation's meaning.

challenges.title: Checking dimensions before multiplication
challenges.description: A small table has 5 examples and 3 measured features per example. If each example is a row, what is its shape?

choices.text: 3 rows by 5 columns.
5 rows by 5 columns.
3 rows by 3 columns.
5 rows by 3 columns.

challenges.hint: Count examples as rows and measurements as columns.

solution.code: 5 rows by 3 columns.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: There are five observations, and each has three feature values.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Reversing counts or making the matrix square does not match the table.

challenges.title: Why feature units matter
challenges.description: A delivery dataset stores distance in kilometers for some records and meters for others, without marking which is which. What is the main risk?

choices.text: The model will automatically convert values to miles.
The target label becomes a feature.
The same number can mean different real distances.
The dataset has no rows.

challenges.hint: Imagine interpreting one number under each unit convention.

solution.code: The same number can mean different real distances.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Without consistent units, a value such as 5 has conflicting meanings.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Standardizing units is needed; inconsistency does not alter labels or row counts automatically.

challenges.title: Finding the mean
challenges.description: A sensor records 4, 6, and 8 degrees. What is the arithmetic mean?

choices.text: 6 degrees.
8 degrees.
18 degrees.
4 degrees.

challenges.hint: Add the readings, then divide by how many there are.

solution.code: 6 degrees.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The sum is 18 and there are 3 readings.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: 18 divided by 3 is 6; 18 is the sum, not the mean.

challenges.title: Median With An Extreme Value
challenges.description: Five sorted repair times are 2, 3, 3, 4, and 40 minutes. What is their median?

choices.text: 10.4 minutes.
40 minutes.
52 minutes.
3 minutes.

challenges.hint: For an odd number of sorted values, locate the one in the middle.

solution.code: 3 minutes.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The third value in the ordered list is 3.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The mean is 10.4, but the median is the central observation, not the total or largest value.

challenges.title: What variance describes
challenges.description: Two delivery routes have the same average time, but one route's times vary much more. Which statistic describes this spread?

choices.text: The mean alone.
Variance.
The row count.
The most common route name.

challenges.hint: The average is known; look for a measure of dispersion.

solution.code: Variance.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Variance summarizes how observations spread around their mean.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The mean describes a center, while a count or category does not measure numeric spread.

challenges.title: Averages and a long tail
challenges.description: A delivery-time histogram shows many short trips and a few very long trips. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The distribution is skewed, so the mean may not describe a typical trip well.
Every trip takes the same time.
Long trips caused the short trips.
The plot proves the route caused delays.

challenges.hint: Separate visible shape from claims about cause.

solution.code: The distribution is skewed, so the mean may not describe a typical trip well.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A few large values alongside many smaller ones create an uneven, long-tailed distribution.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A plot reveals shape, but it cannot establish equal values or identify a cause.

challenges.title: Compare Groups With Box Plots
challenges.description: A manager wants to compare the middle and spread of repair costs at three workshops. Which display is a useful choice?

choices.text: A histogram of workshop names.
A scatter plot of customer IDs against names.
Side-by-side box plots of repair costs by workshop.
A table containing only the largest repair at each workshop.

challenges.hint: Choose a view that summarizes the distribution for each group.

solution.code: Side-by-side box plots of repair costs by workshop.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A box plot shows a center and spread for each workshop, making comparison possible.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A histogram of names or a single maximum does not compare the groups' distributions.

challenges.title: Exploring two numeric variables
challenges.description: An analyst wants to see whether longer delivery distances tend to be associated with longer delivery times. Which plot is a good first choice?

choices.text: A histogram containing only delivery times.
A scatter plot with distance and time as axes.
A box plot of delivery IDs.
A list of customer names.

challenges.hint: Choose a display that places both quantities on axes.

solution.code: A scatter plot with distance and time as axes.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Each point can show one delivery's distance and time, making a possible relationship visible.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A single-variable distribution plot cannot directly show how two measures vary together.

challenges.title: Interpreting a plotted pattern
challenges.description: A scatter plot shows customers receiving more reminders also tend to make more purchases. What can the plot alone establish?

choices.text: Reminders caused every purchase.
No other factor affects purchases.
The measures are identical.
An association worth investigating, not proof reminders caused purchases.

challenges.hint: Separate an observed relationship from its explanation.

solution.code: An association worth investigating, not proof reminders caused purchases.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The plot can show the variables moving together in these records.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Other factors may explain the pattern; a plot alone cannot establish cause.

challenges.title: Using a box plot
challenges.description: A repair-cost box plot shows one point far above the upper whisker. What is the careful interpretation?

choices.text: It proves the record is wrong and must be deleted.
Every repair cost is high.
It flags a potentially unusual value worth checking.
It identifies why the repair was expensive.

challenges.hint: Treat a visual flag as a reason to inspect, not a final decision.

solution.code: It flags a potentially unusual value worth checking.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A distant point may be an outlier relative to the rest of the distribution.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: It may be valid or erroneous; the plot alone cannot decide which or explain why.

challenges.title: Inspect Missingness By Source
challenges.description: A sensor dataset has blanks mostly during night shifts. What should an analyst inspect before choosing how to fill them?

choices.text: Whether missingness is linked to the time or conditions when readings were collected.
Whether the model's training accuracy is already high.
Whether every blank should be treated as a measured zero.
Whether the column name is longer at night.

challenges.hint: Look for a pattern in which records are missing, not just the total number.

solution.code: Whether missingness is linked to the time or conditions when readings were collected.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A concentration of blanks at night may point to a collection or sensor issue.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Knowing the pattern helps choose a defensible policy; zero-filling could hide the cause.

challenges.title: Checking repeated records
challenges.description: A customer export may contain the same transaction twice. What is a useful inspection step?

choices.text: Replace all amounts with zero.
Train a model before checking.
Remove every row with a common weekday.
Look for duplicate transaction IDs or repeated records.

challenges.hint: Use a field or combination of fields that should identify a transaction.

solution.code: Look for duplicate transaction IDs or repeated records.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Repeated identifiers or matching transaction details can reveal duplicated examples.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A common weekday is not evidence of duplication, and changing amounts destroys information.

challenges.title: Checking data types
challenges.description: A column intended for ages includes "27", "unknown", and "thirty". What should inspection reveal?

choices.text: All values are valid integers because they share a column.
The column mixes numeric-looking values with text and needs review.
"Unknown" automatically means age zero.
The prediction threshold is incorrect.

challenges.hint: Compare actual values with the type expected for the field.

solution.code: The column mixes numeric-looking values with text and needs review.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The text entries do not parse consistently as numeric ages.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A shared column does not ensure consistent types; missing and text values need a policy.

challenges.title: Flagging impossible values
challenges.description: A form records a person's age as 240 years. What is the best first response?

choices.text: Flag it as implausible and investigate its source.
Assume every age in the file is wrong.
Treat 240 as a typical age.
Use 240 as the answer for every record.

challenges.hint: Check whether the value falls within a plausible range for its field.

solution.code: Flag it as implausible and investigate its source.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: An age of 240 is unusual enough to check for entry or unit errors.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Flagging is not the same as discarding the dataset or replacing every observation.

challenges.title: Prediction Output Types
challenges.description: A model returns a delay probability of 0.3 for a package. What form of output is 0.3?

choices.text: The confirmed delay outcome.
A measurement of the package's weight.
A numeric probability estimate from the model.
A guarantee that the delivery will be late.

challenges.hint: Separate the number the model produced from the later real-world outcome.

solution.code: A numeric probability estimate from the model.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The value 0.3 is a model estimate of likelihood, not an observed delivery result.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: It is neither the package's weight nor a guarantee that a delay will or will not occur.

challenges.title: Probability and class decision
challenges.description: A message classifier outputs a spam probability of 0.72. What additional choice is needed for a yes-or-no flag?

choices.text: A new row for every word.
A decision threshold.
Conversion of the score to a delivery time.
A guarantee that the message is spam.

challenges.hint: A score can be compared with a cutoff to make a discrete decision.

solution.code: A decision threshold.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The probability is an output; a threshold determines which scores trigger the spam label.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A score does not guarantee the outcome or require changing the prediction task.

challenges.title: Interpreting a model score
challenges.description: A model gives a customer a risk score of 0.8. What is the safest immediate interpretation?

choices.text: There is certainly an 80% chance of harm in every case.
The customer must be rejected automatically.
The score is the customer's observed outcome.
It is a model output whose meaning depends on its definition and validation.

challenges.hint: Do not assume a numeric score is automatically a calibrated probability or action.

solution.code: It is a model output whose meaning depends on its definition and validation.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The model produces a score; validation is needed to understand what it represents.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A decision depends on task, calibration, threshold, and consequences, not the number alone.

challenges.title: Labels From Observed Outcomes
challenges.description: A dataset's labels say whether invoices were paid late, based on the recorded payment dates. Why are these labels more useful than guesses made before payment?

choices.text: They guarantee every future invoice will be paid on time.
They are available as input features before the payment date.
They describe outcomes that actually occurred.
They remove the need to inspect the data.

challenges.hint: A target should represent the outcome the model is meant to learn.

solution.code: They describe outcomes that actually occurred.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Recorded payment dates let the team determine whether each invoice was late.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Observed outcomes give a consistent target for training; they do not predict or guarantee future cases.

challenges.title: Grouping without supplied labels
challenges.description: A museum has visitor activity records but no predefined categories and asks a program to group similar patterns. What kind of learning is used?

choices.text: Unsupervised learning.
Supervised classification from known categories.
Regression to a supplied numeric target.
A rule assigning everyone to one group.

challenges.hint: Notice that no desired category is supplied for each record.

solution.code: Unsupervised learning.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The program is finding structure in examples without labeled group names.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Clusters still need human interpretation; classification and regression need target labels.

challenges.title: Interpreting discovered clusters
challenges.description: A clustering tool separates shoppers into three groups, but the groups have no descriptions. What is the right next step?

choices.text: Assume their names are "good," "average," and "bad."
Treat group numbers as confirmed outcomes.
Claim the groups prove why shoppers behave differently.
Inspect whether groups are stable and useful, then interpret their patterns.

challenges.hint: A grouping algorithm does not automatically provide meaningful names.

solution.code: Inspect whether groups are stable and useful, then interpret their patterns.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Reviewing members' characteristics can help describe what distinguishes each cluster.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Cluster IDs have no inherent business meaning and do not prove causal explanations.

challenges.title: Checking Cluster Stability
challenges.description: A team finds customer groups in one sample of activity records. What can it check to see whether the grouping is dependable?

choices.text: Whether each group number is a confirmed customer label.
Whether similar groups appear when it analyzes another sample of records.
Whether the group names are sorted alphabetically.
Whether the model predicts a numeric target that was never supplied.

challenges.hint: A useful pattern should not depend entirely on one particular sample.

solution.code: Whether similar groups appear when it analyzes another sample of records.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Comparing results across samples can reveal whether the group structure is stable.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Cluster IDs are not supplied ground-truth labels; stability is a separate check from naming groups.

challenges.title: Available-at-decision-time features
challenges.description: A clinic predicts whether a patient will need a follow-up visit using information recorded before the appointment ends. Which candidate is valid then?

choices.text: The patient's age recorded at check-in.
Whether a follow-up happened next week.
The final billing code entered afterward.
Next month's model evaluation score.

challenges.hint: Use only information available when the prediction is made.

solution.code: The patient's age recorded at check-in.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Age is known at check-in and can be an input then.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Later events and evaluation results occur after the prediction time and leak future information.

challenges.title: Avoiding future information
challenges.description: A model predicts at dispatch whether a package will arrive late. Which input is unfairly easy because it is recorded only after delivery?

choices.text: Package weight at dispatch.
Destination known at dispatch.
The final delivery timestamp.
Planned shipping service.

challenges.hint: Compare when each value becomes available with prediction time.

solution.code: The final delivery timestamp.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The final delivery timestamp reveals the outcome after arrival.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Weight, destination, and planned service can be known before the eventual outcome.

challenges.title: Route Support Messages
challenges.description: A help desk wants to send written questions to the right team based on what each message is about. Which broad AI use case fits?

choices.text: Image inspection.
Language understanding.
Numeric price estimation.
Clustering without labels.

challenges.hint: The system must interpret written messages before routing them.

solution.code: Language understanding.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Identifying a message's topic or intent uses language understanding.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The task is not examining pictures, predicting a numeric amount, or discovering unlabeled groups.

challenges.title: A useful feature versus an identifier
challenges.description: A random record number is assigned only to keep rows distinct. What should a team avoid assuming?

choices.text: That it helps identify one row in the file.
That it may help match records during cleaning.
That it can be excluded from model inputs.
That it is automatically a meaningful predictive feature.

challenges.hint: Distinguish bookkeeping purpose from information about the outcome.

solution.code: That it is automatically a meaningful predictive feature.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A random identifier usually encodes record identity rather than a meaningful predictive pattern.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: It may help track rows, but usefulness for data management does not make it a model feature.

challenges.title: Standardizing inconsistent categories
challenges.description: A city column contains "North Bay", "north bay", and "N. Bay", all intended to name one place. What is a suitable cleaning goal?

choices.text: Treat each spelling as a different city without checking.
Replace city names with the label value.
Use one consistent representation for the same city.
Convert every entry to a random string.

challenges.hint: Find values that differ in form but may mean the same thing.

solution.code: Use one consistent representation for the same city.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Standardizing equivalent spellings prevents one category being split into several apparent ones.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Confirm equivalence, then choose a consistent representation instead of inventing new meanings.

challenges.title: Handling missing measurements
challenges.description: A temperature column has blanks. What should a data team do before choosing how to handle them?

choices.text: Determine why values are missing and select an appropriate policy.
Always replace each blank with zero.
Copy the previous row into every blank.
Delete the column without checking its importance.

challenges.hint: A blank may have different meanings depending on collection.

solution.code: Determine why values are missing and select an appropriate policy.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Knowing why values are absent helps choose whether to fill, flag, or exclude them.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Zero or a neighboring value can mislead; dropping the column may discard useful data.

challenges.title: Distinguish Repeat Orders From Duplicates
challenges.description: Two records share a customer and product but have different order IDs and amounts. What should the data cleaner do?

choices.text: Delete one because matching customer and product always means duplicate.
Merge their amounts and discard both IDs.
Replace both records with a missing value.
Keep them unless evidence shows they are the same transaction.

challenges.hint: Repeated customers can make separate legitimate purchases.

solution.code: Keep them unless evidence shows they are the same transaction.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Different order IDs and amounts suggest these may be distinct transactions.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Deduplication should use evidence about record identity, not just repeated customer or product values.

challenges.title: Retain Verified Rare Values
challenges.description: A shipment weight looks unusually high, but the source confirms it was a valid bulk order. What is the sensible cleaning choice?

choices.text: Delete it solely because it is far from the average.
Keep the verified value and account for its rarity when analyzing the data.
Replace it with zero so it cannot affect a model.
Copy it into every other shipment record.

challenges.hint: Unusual does not mean incorrect once the source has been checked.

solution.code: Keep the verified value and account for its rarity when analyzing the data.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The confirmed bulk order is a real example, even if it is rare.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Removing valid extremes can erase useful cases and distort what the data represents.

challenges.title: Clarify Ambiguous Dates
challenges.description: A file contains dates like 04/05/2026, but the source does not say whether the order is month/day or day/month. What should the team do before standardizing them?

choices.text: Confirm the source's date convention so the values are parsed correctly.
Choose a convention at random and apply it to every row.
Replace all ambiguous dates with today's date.
Treat every date as a numeric label.

challenges.hint: The same string can represent different calendar dates under different conventions.

solution.code: Confirm the source's date convention so the values are parsed correctly.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: 04/05/2026 is ambiguous without knowing how the source writes dates.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Confirming the convention avoids silently changing the meaning during cleaning.

challenges.title: Raising A Classification Threshold
challenges.description: A transaction is flagged as fraud when its risk score is at least a chosen cutoff. If the team raises that cutoff, what is a likely effect?

choices.text: Every transaction will be flagged as fraud.
The model will change its output into a dollar amount.
Fewer transactions will be flagged, including possibly fewer legitimate ones.
The number of fraud cases in the data will increase.

challenges.hint: A higher cutoff requires a stronger score before a case is flagged.

solution.code: Fewer transactions will be flagged, including possibly fewer legitimate ones.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Some scores that previously met the lower cutoff will now fall below it.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: This changes the decision rule and its tradeoff, not the underlying transactions or target values.

challenges.title: Recognizing multiple classes
challenges.description: A plant app assigns a photo to one of five known flower species. Which task is this?

choices.text: Regression to a continuous flower value.
Classification with multiple classes.
Unsupervised grouping with no known categories.
Estimating an average of five image files.

challenges.hint: The output is one category chosen from known names.

solution.code: Classification with multiple classes.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Five species are discrete labels, so predicting among them is classification.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The category count makes it multi-class, not regression or unlabeled clustering.

challenges.title: Choosing a classification threshold
challenges.description: A spam filter's main priority is not to block legitimate urgent messages, even if some spam gets through. What should guide its threshold?

choices.text: A rule that every probability uses 0.5.
The number of characters in each subject.
Whether training data was a spreadsheet.
The relative costs of false alarms and missed spam.

challenges.hint: A cutoff controls how readily the system flags a message.

solution.code: The relative costs of false alarms and missed spam.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Changing the cutoff changes the balance between blocking legitimate mail and missing spam.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The preferred tradeoff depends on consequences; one fixed cutoff is not always best.

challenges.title: Probability is not certainty
challenges.description: A weather classifier assigns a 0.9 probability to rain tomorrow. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Rain is guaranteed.
It will rain for exactly 90% of the day.
It is a high estimated chance, not certainty.
The value proves every forecast is accurate.

challenges.hint: Interpret the number as an estimate rather than a promise.

solution.code: It is a high estimated chance, not certainty.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A probability of 0.9 represents a high estimated likelihood under the model's interpretation.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Even a high probability can be wrong and says nothing about rain duration or accuracy on every case.

challenges.title: Understanding a false positive
challenges.description: A filter flags a legitimate message as spam. What mistake has it made?

choices.text: A false positive.
A false negative.
A correct negative prediction.
A regression error in minutes.

challenges.hint: Compare the predicted class with the message's actual class.

solution.code: A false positive.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The model predicted spam, but the message is actually legitimate.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A false negative would miss actual spam; this is a positive flag on a negative example.

challenges.title: False Negative Example
challenges.description: A spam message reaches the inbox because a filter classified it as legitimate. What kind of mistake did the filter make?

choices.text: A false positive.
A correct positive prediction.
A regression error.
A false negative.

challenges.hint: Compare the message's actual class with the class the filter predicted.

solution.code: A false negative.

steps.title: Compare prediction and outcome
steps.explanation: The message is actually spam, but the filter predicted the negative class, legitimate.

steps.title: Name the error
steps.explanation: Missing a real positive case is a false negative; flagging a legitimate message would be a false positive.

challenges.title: Direction Of A Regression Error
challenges.description: A repair-cost model predicts $210, and the final bill is $230. What happened on this example?

choices.text: The model overpredicted by $20.
The model underpredicted by $20.
The prediction was exactly correct.
The error is 20 percent by definition.

challenges.hint: Compare the estimate with the larger observed bill.

solution.code: The model underpredicted by $20.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The observed bill exceeds the prediction by $20.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Because the prediction was lower than the outcome, it is an underprediction; a percent error needs a specified calculation.

challenges.title: What a prediction error compares
challenges.description: A model predicts 50 minutes for a trip that actually takes 57 minutes. What does its prediction error compare?

choices.text: The predicted value with the observed value.
Two input features with each other.
The model name with the dataset name.
Training and test row counts.

challenges.hint: Use the prediction and later measured outcome in the scenario.

solution.code: The predicted value with the observed value.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The difference between 57 and 50 shows how far this estimate missed travel time.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Prediction error concerns output versus target, not names, input relationships, or partition sizes.

challenges.title: Interpreting mean absolute error
challenges.description: A model's mean absolute error for delivery time is 6 minutes. What does this communicate?

choices.text: Every prediction misses by exactly 6 minutes.
The model is correct 6 percent of the time.
The average absolute prediction miss is 6 minutes.
Average delivery itself lasts 6 minutes.

challenges.hint: The metric summarizes magnitudes of prediction errors across examples.

solution.code: The average absolute prediction miss is 6 minutes.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: MAE averages the size of prediction-versus-observation differences without their signs.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: It does not mean every case has the same error, nor measure duration or percent correct.

challenges.title: Why RMSE notices large misses
challenges.description: Two forecasting models have similar typical errors, but one makes a few much larger mistakes. Which metric is especially sensitive to those?

choices.text: The number of dataset columns.
Root mean squared error (RMSE).
The median feature name.
The count of training rows alone.

challenges.hint: Think about which metric squares deviations before combining them.

solution.code: Root mean squared error (RMSE).

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Squaring makes larger deviations contribute disproportionately to mean squared error and its square root.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: RMSE therefore responds strongly to occasional large misses compared with a count or label.

challenges.title: Choosing An Error Metric In Units
challenges.description: A team predicts package weights and wants an easy-to-read average error in kilograms that does not emphasize a few large misses as strongly as RMSE. Which metric is a reasonable choice?

choices.text: Classification accuracy.
The number of feature columns.
The largest observed weight.
Mean absolute error (MAE).

challenges.hint: Choose a regression metric expressed in the target's units and based on absolute misses.

solution.code: Mean absolute error (MAE).

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: MAE averages absolute prediction errors, so its result is interpretable in kilograms.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Accuracy is for class predictions, while a column count or maximum is not an average prediction-error measure.

challenges.title: Evaluating a forecast fairly
challenges.description: A team trains on older daily sales to predict next month. Which holdout strategy best matches this use?

choices.text: Mix past and future records without regard to date.
Evaluate only on training days.
Reserve a later period after the training period.
Choose records after seeing which predictions look best.

challenges.hint: Preserve the order in which the model would encounter data.

solution.code: Reserve a later period after the training period.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A later period tests whether patterns learned from the past help predict the future.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Mixing future records into training or reusing examples makes evaluation unrealistically favorable.

challenges.title: Defining a useful outcome
challenges.description: A team wants to "use AI to improve deliveries." What is a useful first step before selecting a model?

choices.text: Specify the decision and measurable outcome that counts as improvement.
Pick the most complex model available.
Deploy before deciding how success will be measured.
Choose a metric only after seeing test results.

challenges.hint: Turn the broad wish into a concrete question and success condition.

solution.code: Specify the decision and measurable outcome that counts as improvement.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A defined outcome clarifies what prediction or decision the system must support.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Without agreed measures, the team cannot tell whether a model or deployment actually helps.

challenges.title: Why begin with a baseline
challenges.description: A team considers an elaborate model to forecast daily orders. Why compare against a simple baseline first?

choices.text: To prove a simple model is always best.
To avoid measuring on held-out data.
To make the target value unnecessary.
To find out whether added complexity improves on a straightforward reference.

challenges.hint: A reference gives the complex approach something concrete to beat.

solution.code: To find out whether added complexity improves on a straightforward reference.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A baseline sets an initial performance level using a simple, understandable method.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The comparison can show whether complexity is worthwhile; it does not predetermine the winner.

challenges.title: Preparing data in a workflow
challenges.description: A project has defined its goal and collected records, but dates are inconsistent and some values missing. What generally comes before fitting?

choices.text: Deploy an unfinished model and repair data later.
Inspect and prepare the data using appropriate cleaning steps.
Use final test outcomes as input features.
Skip review because training code parses everything.

challenges.hint: Ensure inputs are trustworthy and represented consistently before training.

solution.code: Inspect and prepare the data using appropriate cleaning steps.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Inspection can expose missingness, type problems, and inconsistent formats.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Ignoring these risks unreliable fitting; held-out outcomes must not become input features.

challenges.title: Respond To Weak Evaluation
challenges.description: A model performs poorly on its evaluation examples. What is a sensible workflow response before launch?

choices.text: Investigate the data and approach, then improve and evaluate again.
Deploy immediately because training finished.
Hide the evaluation and report training performance only.
Change evaluation labels until the score improves.

challenges.hint: Treat evaluation as evidence to guide the next iteration.

solution.code: Investigate the data and approach, then improve and evaluate again.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Weak results may point to data problems, an unsuitable approach, or a need to revisit the goal.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A responsible workflow uses evidence to improve and recheck rather than concealing results or changing answers.

challenges.title: What Deployment Means
challenges.description: A model file has been trained and saved, but no application or user can send it inputs or receive predictions. What is still missing?

choices.text: Another copy of the training rows.
A new label for every feature.
Putting the model into a usable system or workflow.
A plot of the training filenames.

challenges.hint: Think about what must happen for a trained model to support a real decision.

solution.code: Putting the model into a usable system or workflow.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Deployment makes the model available through an application, service, or other practical workflow.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Saving the artifact alone does not make it usable by the people or processes it is meant to support.

challenges.title: Why monitor a deployed model
challenges.description: A package-delay predictor is in use. Why should the team continue monitoring it?

choices.text: Monitoring guarantees no future prediction is wrong.
Data and outcomes can change, so performance may drift after launch.
Monitoring removes the need to collect outcomes.
A deployed model never encounters new situations.

challenges.hint: Consider whether the world and input patterns remain fixed after deployment.

solution.code: Data and outcomes can change, so performance may drift after launch.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: New routes, seasons, or practices can change relationships between inputs and delays.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Monitoring can reveal problems but cannot guarantee correctness or replace outcome data.

challenges.title: What to watch in production
challenges.description: An invoice model predicts late payment, but labels arrive weeks later. What is practical monitoring?

choices.text: Assume perfect accuracy until a user complains.
Use model predictions as confirmed outcomes.
Stop checking once deployed.
Track input patterns now and review performance when outcomes arrive.

challenges.hint: Some warning signals are available before the true target is known.

solution.code: Track input patterns now and review performance when outcomes arrive.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Input shifts can be monitored promptly; correctness can be checked once payment outcomes arrive.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Predictions are not ground truth, so delayed labels are still needed to measure performance.

challenges.title: Workflow continues after launch
challenges.description: A team evaluated and deployed a model. Which statement best describes the remaining workflow?

choices.text: Assume the original evaluation is valid forever.
Delete training data so the model cannot be checked.
Continue monitoring and respond to evidence about changing performance.
Treat deployment as proof of business success.

challenges.hint: A deployed system continues to face new data and operating conditions.

solution.code: Continue monitoring and respond to evidence about changing performance.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Monitoring can reveal whether the model still meets its success criteria.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Launch does not guarantee lasting performance or impact; evidence may call for investigation.

challenges.title: Understanding Written Feedback
challenges.description: A store wants to group written reviews into themes such as delivery complaints and product praise. Which broad AI use case is most relevant?

choices.text: Language understanding.
Visual defect inspection.
Forecasting future temperatures.
Measuring the mean of review lengths.

challenges.hint: The evidence to interpret is the meaning of written comments.

solution.code: Language understanding.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Finding themes in reviews requires processing and interpreting language.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The task is not image inspection or numeric forecasting; review length alone misses the requested meaning.

challenges.title: Recognizing a fraud-detection task
challenges.description: A bank flags card transactions that may be fraudulent so staff can review them. Which use case is this?

choices.text: Language translation.
Demand forecasting.
Product recommendation.
Fraud detection.

challenges.hint: The system identifies suspicious activity for follow-up.

solution.code: Fraud detection.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Flagging potentially fraudulent transactions is a fraud-detection use case.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Translation changes language, forecasting estimates future quantities, and recommendations suggest items.

challenges.title: Matching image inspection
challenges.description: A factory identifies visible cracks in photographs of manufactured parts. Which application fits?

choices.text: A text-only sentiment summary.
Visual inspection using image data.
A demand forecast from sales history.
Grouping customers by purchases.

challenges.hint: The evidence the system must examine is in pictures.

solution.code: Visual inspection using image data.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Detecting visible defects from photographs is an image-based inspection task.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The other options concern language, numeric forecasting, or customer segmentation.

challenges.title: Why AI tasks need different evaluation
challenges.description: A team compares a fraud flagger, demand forecast, and camera-based defect checker. Why may one shared evaluation measure be unsuitable?

choices.text: Their outputs, error costs, and operational needs differ.
All AI systems return the same output type.
Every task uses identical examples and labels.
Evaluation is unnecessary once any model is accurate.

challenges.hint: Compare what each system predicts and what happens when it is wrong.

solution.code: Their outputs, error costs, and operational needs differ.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A missed fraud event, a stock forecast error, and an overlooked defect have different consequences.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Evaluation should match task targets and use; one generic measure may hide important failures.

challenges.title: Why plot data before fitting
challenges.description: An analyst plots sales amounts before choosing a model and notices a few exceptionally large orders. Why is this useful?

choices.text: It proves the large orders are mistakes.
It guarantees the eventual model predicts correctly.
It reveals distribution details that may affect data checks and modeling choices.
It replaces the need to define the goal.

challenges.hint: A plot can guide investigation without settling every question.

solution.code: It reveals distribution details that may affect data checks and modeling choices.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Extreme values can prompt the analyst to check records and understand the distribution shape.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Visualization is exploratory evidence, not proof of error or a guarantee of model quality.

challenges.title: Inspection informs cleaning
challenges.description: A dataset has blanks, repeated rows, and extreme measurements. Why inspect before applying changes?

choices.text: Every unusual cell should always become zero.
Different issues may need different treatments based on what they mean.
Inspection makes the target unnecessary.
Cleaning is useful only after deployment.

challenges.hint: A sound cleaning choice depends on what an anomaly represents.

solution.code: Different issues may need different treatments based on what they mean.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Missing values, accidental duplicates, and legitimate extremes are distinct situations.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: One blanket replacement can corrupt valid data; inspection guides an appropriate action.

challenges.title: Consistent target labels
challenges.description: Two reviewers label the same kind of request "urgent" or "normal" using different personal rules. What is the key problem for supervised training?

choices.text: The dataset has too many feature columns.
The model cannot read any text at all.
The reviewers created a histogram.
Labels may be inconsistent, giving the learner conflicting examples.

challenges.hint: A learner needs the target to mean the same thing across examples.

solution.code: Labels may be inconsistent, giving the learner conflicting examples.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Inconsistent labeling makes equivalent cases carry different answers during training.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A shared definition improves target quality; feature count or visualization does not fix contradictory labels.

challenges.title: Prediction timing defines usable inputs
challenges.description: A school predicts attendance before the morning begins. Which candidate should be excluded if it is recorded only at day's end?

choices.text: The student's enrolled grade.
The day of the week.
Whether the student actually attended that day.
The weather forecast available that morning.

challenges.hint: Check whether each value exists at the intended decision time.

solution.code: Whether the student actually attended that day.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Actual attendance is the outcome and is not known before the day ends.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Grade, weekday, and an available forecast can be known beforehand, unlike the eventual target.

challenges.title: Consistent Input Preparation
challenges.description: A model is trained after dates are standardized, but the live service sends dates in several raw formats. What should the team do?

choices.text: Apply consistent preparation so live inputs match the form used during training.
Assume the model will infer every date format correctly.
Use the final outcome as a substitute for the date.
Remove all dates from training without checking their role.

challenges.hint: Compare how the same feature is represented during training and use.

solution.code: Apply consistent preparation so live inputs match the form used during training.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A model can receive inconsistent or invalid inputs if live dates are not prepared consistently.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Keeping preparation consistent reduces avoidable input errors; guessing formats or discarding data blindly is unsafe.

challenges.title: Range As A Spread Summary
challenges.description: Three daily order counts are 12, 18, and 30. What is the range of these values?

choices.text: 20 orders.
60 orders.
12 orders.
18 orders.

challenges.hint: Subtract the smallest observation from the largest.

solution.code: 18 orders.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The maximum is 30 and the minimum is 12.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: 30 minus 12 is 18; the sum is 60 and the mean is 20.

challenges.title: Calculate Absolute Prediction Error
challenges.description: A demand model predicts 42 orders, and the store later sells 37. What is the absolute error for this prediction?

choices.text: -5 orders.
5 orders.
37 orders.
79 orders.

challenges.hint: Take the size of the difference without keeping its direction.

solution.code: 5 orders.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The prediction and observation differ by 42 - 37 = 5.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Absolute error is nonnegative; the signed difference and sum are not the requested magnitude.

challenges.title: Communicating a numeric estimate
challenges.description: A store model estimates tomorrow's demand at 200 items. What should a user avoid inferring from this prediction alone?

choices.text: That demand is guaranteed to be exactly 200.
That 200 is the model's current numeric estimate.
That the estimate can be compared with later demand.
That the value may inform a stocking decision.

challenges.hint: A point estimate is a model output, not a promise.

solution.code: That demand is guaranteed to be exactly 200.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The model outputs 200, but actual demand may differ.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Treating it as guaranteed ignores uncertainty; comparing with outcomes later helps assess usefulness.

challenges.title: Plotting category frequencies
challenges.description: A school compares student counts in four known transport categories. Which display is a natural starting point?

choices.text: A scatter plot with student names on both axes.
A histogram of category names as numeric intervals.
A bar chart of counts by category.
A line plot connecting unrelated student IDs.

challenges.hint: The variable is categorical, and the question asks for counts per category.

solution.code: A bar chart of counts by category.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A bar chart can show a count for each named transport category.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A histogram is intended for numeric ranges; the other plots do not communicate these category totals clearly.

challenges.title: Identify the form of a prediction
challenges.description: A model returns "blue" for a shirt image. What form of prediction is this?

choices.text: A continuous numeric estimate.
A class label.
A measured probability of 0.8.
The size of the training dataset.

challenges.hint: Look at the kind of value the model returned.

solution.code: A class label.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: "Blue" is a category assigned to the input image.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: It is not a numeric estimate or probability unless the system separately returns a score.

challenges.title: Language Understanding Example
challenges.description: A voice assistant interprets a spoken request such as "set a timer for ten minutes." Which broad capability is central?

choices.text: Unsupervised grouping of customer records.
Regression of a house price.
Visual inspection of a product surface.
Language understanding.

challenges.hint: The system must interpret a person's spoken words.

solution.code: Language understanding.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Understanding the command's meaning is a language task.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The request is not a numeric house-price estimate, an unlabeled grouping, or an image inspection.

challenges.title: Zero Versus Missing
challenges.description: A survey records a rating of 0 for one response and leaves another response blank. What should cleaning preserve?

choices.text: Replace both entries with the average rating.
Assume the blank means the same as a genuine zero in every dataset.
Treat zero as a recorded value and the blank as missing unless the data definition says otherwise.
Delete all responses with ratings below the mean.

challenges.hint: A recorded zero and an absent value are not automatically the same thing.

solution.code: Treat zero as a recorded value and the blank as missing unless the data definition says otherwise.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Zero is an observed number, whereas a blank indicates no recorded response.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Collapsing them can erase meaning; follow the field definition when selecting a cleaning policy.

challenges.title: Translation As Language Use Case
challenges.description: A service converts a customer's written message from Spanish into English for an agent. Which broad AI capability is being used?

choices.text: Language understanding and processing.
Visual inspection of product defects.
Unsupervised grouping of numeric measurements.
Regression estimating a continuous price.

challenges.hint: The input and output are human language.

solution.code: Language understanding and processing.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Translating a message requires processing its language content.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The task is not analyzing images, finding numeric clusters, or predicting a price.

challenges.title: Why a workflow uses feedback
challenges.description: After launch, outcomes show a model misses more late packages on a newly added route. What is a sensible response?

choices.text: Ignore results because deployment already happened.
Change old predictions to match new outcomes.
Assume every route now has the same delay pattern.
Investigate the change and use evidence to decide whether updates are needed.

challenges.hint: Monitoring is valuable when it leads to a careful response to evidence.

solution.code: Investigate the change and use evidence to decide whether updates are needed.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The new route may represent a changed pattern worth investigating with relevant data.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Evidence may guide checks or updates; it does not justify ignoring results or rewriting history.

challenges.title: Classify Review Sentiment
challenges.description: A feedback tool assigns each written review one of two known labels: positive or negative. What kind of prediction is this?

choices.text: Regression of a continuous quantity.
Binary classification.
Unsupervised grouping without known labels.
Calculation of the review column average.

challenges.hint: Check whether the requested output is one of two supplied categories or a numeric amount.

solution.code: Binary classification.

steps.title: Identify the output
steps.explanation: Positive and negative are two distinct target categories for each review.

steps.title: Choose the task type
steps.explanation: Predicting one of two known classes is binary classification, not a numeric estimate or unlabeled grouping.

challenges.title: Reading Text From Forms
challenges.description: A service scans handwritten application forms and extracts the written names and dates. Which input type is central to this task?

choices.text: Images containing text that must be interpreted.
A future sales forecast.
A list of model accuracy scores.
A set of unlabeled customer clusters.

challenges.hint: The original evidence is a picture of a filled-in form.

solution.code: Images containing text that must be interpreted.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: The system must examine image data and interpret the text written in it.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Sales forecasts, evaluation scores, and customer groupings do not provide the form contents.

challenges.title: Metrics depend on the objective
challenges.description: A system ranks possible fraud cases for human review, but reviewers inspect only 20 per hour. What should evaluation consider?

choices.text: Whether every transaction is predicted suspicious.
Whether the source code has the longest title.
Whether the top-ranked cases help reviewers find suspicious transactions within their capacity.
Whether training has exactly 20 rows.

challenges.hint: Connect evaluation to how the system is actually used.

solution.code: Whether the top-ranked cases help reviewers find suspicious transactions within their capacity.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A useful ranking places valuable cases where reviewers can examine them.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The capacity limit makes ranking quality relevant; predicting everything or matching row counts is not success.

challenges.title: Evaluation data should match use
challenges.description: A photo checker will inspect products under dim factory lighting but was evaluated only on bright studio photos. What is the main concern?

choices.text: The model is guaranteed to fail on every factory photo.
Evaluation examples may not represent real-use conditions.
Lighting cannot affect image inputs.
Studio photos automatically count as future outcomes.

challenges.hint: Compare the evaluation setting with the environment of actual predictions.

solution.code: Evaluation examples may not represent real-use conditions.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: Lighting differences may change images and make the evaluation less representative.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The gap calls for a relevant test, not proof of total failure or proof that lighting is irrelevant.

challenges.title: Why inspect actual records
challenges.description: A summary says a dataset has few missing values. Why might an analyst still sample actual records before training?

choices.text: Sampling proves every remaining value is correct.
Individual rows replace the need to check counts.
A summary always contains every formatting problem.
A small count can hide an important pattern or malformed examples.

challenges.hint: Aggregate counts may not show what is happening in particular examples.

solution.code: A small count can hide an important pattern or malformed examples.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A sample can reveal whether missingness or unusual formats are concentrated or meaningful.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Inspecting rows complements summaries; neither guarantees that every record is error-free.

challenges.title: Opposite Errors Can Cancel
challenges.description: One model predicts 10 units too high on one order and 10 units too low on another. Why can mean absolute error be more informative than the average signed error here?

choices.text: Absolute error changes the predictions into class labels.
Signed errors always show the correct future outcome.
The signed errors cancel, while absolute errors retain the size of both misses.
The two misses should be removed from the evaluation.

challenges.hint: Compare adding the signed differences with adding their magnitudes.

solution.code: The signed errors cancel, while absolute errors retain the size of both misses.

steps.title: Trace the example
steps.explanation: A positive error and an equal negative error sum to zero when signs are kept.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Taking absolute values makes both misses count as 10-unit errors rather than hiding them through cancellation.

challenges.title: Linear regression output
challenges.description: A linear regression model uses floor area to estimate house price. What kind of target does it predict in this task?

choices.text: A numeric price.
A cluster ID with no target.
A prewritten decision-tree rule.
A sequence of words.

challenges.hint: Look at the value the model is asked to estimate.

solution.code: A numeric price.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The target is a numeric amount: the house's price.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Linear regression models a numeric target; it does not require the target to be a category.

challenges.title: From probability to decision
challenges.description: A binary logistic regression model gives an email a spam probability of 0.8. With a spam threshold of 0.5, which class is predicted?

choices.text: No class can be selected from a probability.
Spam.
Not spam.
Both classes at once.

challenges.hint: Compare the score with the stated threshold.

solution.code: Spam.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The score 0.8 is above the 0.5 threshold, so the decision is spam.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: A probability is a score; the threshold turns it into a class decision.

challenges.title: Holding out the test set
