challenges.description: Why keep a test set separate until the model and its settings have been chosen?

choices.text: To guarantee equal accuracy for every future group.
To choose the best hyperparameters repeatedly on the test set.
To estimate performance on data not used for training or model selection.
To give the model more training examples.

challenges.hint: The final check should use data not involved in choosing the model.

solution.code: To estimate performance on data not used for training or model selection.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: An untouched test set provides a final check after model selection.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Repeatedly choosing settings based on test results makes that estimate less independent.

challenges.title: Measuring missed cases
challenges.description: A screening model identifies 8 of 10 actual positive cases. What is its recall for the positive class?

choices.text: Recall cannot be calculated without the number of true negatives.

challenges.hint: Recall divides detected positives by all actual positives.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Recall is 8 / 10 = 0.8.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: True negatives are not needed for this calculation; missed positives are included in the denominator.

challenges.title: Distances in k-NN
challenges.description: A k-NN model uses age in years and annual income in dollars. Why might scaling the features help?

choices.text: It can prevent the larger numeric scale of income from dominating distance.
It guarantees the nearest neighbors have the correct label.
It turns the problem into unsupervised learning.
It removes the need to choose k.

challenges.hint: Consider how numeric units affect a distance calculation.

solution.code: It can prevent the larger numeric scale of income from dominating distance.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Without scaling, dollar differences can be much larger numerically than age differences.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Scaling affects distances but does not guarantee accurate predictions or choose k.

challenges.title: A tree that memorizes
challenges.description: A decision tree has near-perfect training accuracy but much lower validation accuracy. Which change is a reasonable way to reduce overfitting?

choices.text: Remove the held-out validation set.
Limit the tree's depth and evaluate again.
Increase its depth without validation.
Train it on the validation labels.

challenges.hint: Consider whether the tree is too flexible for the training data.

solution.code: Limit the tree's depth and evaluate again.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Limiting depth can prevent a tree from learning very specific training-set rules.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The effect must still be checked on validation data; a shallower tree is not automatically best.

challenges.title: Preparing a category
challenges.description: A model expects numeric inputs, but a column contains the categories red, blue, and green. What preprocessing can represent the categories without imposing an arbitrary numeric order?

choices.text: Using the test labels as category values.
Sorting the categories and assuming their numbers express distance.
One-hot encoding.
Replacing every category with the same number.

challenges.hint: Create separate indicators rather than inventing a ranking.

solution.code: One-hot encoding.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: One-hot encoding creates indicator columns for the categories.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Assigning arbitrary integers can suggest an order or distance that the categories do not have.

challenges.title: Creating a useful feature
challenges.description: For a sales forecast made each morning, which engineered feature uses only information already available?

choices.text: The current day's final sales.
Tomorrow's sales.
The final test set's average target.
Total sales from the previous day.

challenges.hint: Check the prediction time before choosing a feature.

solution.code: Total sales from the previous day.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Yesterday's completed sales are available when the morning forecast is made.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The current day's final sales and tomorrow's sales are future information at that point.

challenges.title: Exploring customer groups
challenges.description: You have customer purchase histories but no group labels. Which approach can help explore groups with similar histories?

choices.text: Clustering the customer records.
Training a classifier on nonexistent group labels.
Calculating classification recall against nonexistent labels.
Using the final test labels as features.

challenges.hint: The goal is to find structure without known group labels.

solution.code: Clustering the customer records.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Clustering groups examples according to a chosen representation and similarity measure.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The resulting groups still need inspection to determine whether they are useful.

challenges.title: PCA and dimensions
challenges.description: What does PCA seek when it constructs the first principal component?

choices.text: A separate class label for every observation.
A direction capturing as much variance as possible in the input data.
The direction that always gives the highest classification accuracy.
A feature guaranteed to be a cause of the target.

challenges.hint: PCA focuses on variation in the inputs, not necessarily prediction labels.

solution.code: A direction capturing as much variance as possible in the input data.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The first principal component is the direction of maximum input variance.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: High variance does not guarantee that a component is most useful for predicting a target.

challenges.title: Fitting preprocessing
challenges.description: When evaluating a model with a train/test split, where should you fit a numeric scaler?

choices.text: On the test set only.
On the test labels.
On the training set, then apply it to both training and test sets.
On the combined training and test sets before splitting.

challenges.hint: Keep information from the test set out of fitted preprocessing.

solution.code: On the training set, then apply it to both training and test sets.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The scaler's parameters should be learned from the training data.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Fitting on test data leaks information from the evaluation set into the workflow.

challenges.title: Recognizing overfitting
challenges.description: A model scores 99% on its training set and 65% on a representative validation set. What is the most direct concern?

choices.text: It has proved it will score 99% on new data.
It cannot make predictions.
Its validation set has become training data automatically.
It may be overfitting the training data.

challenges.hint: Compare performance on seen and unseen examples.

solution.code: It may be overfitting the training data.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The large gap suggests the model fits training examples much better than held-out ones.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The gap is a warning to investigate, not proof of a particular underlying cause.

challenges.title: Rotating validation folds
challenges.description: What happens in five-fold cross-validation?

choices.text: Each fold is used once for validation while the other four are used for training.
All five folds are used for training in every run.
One fold is always used for validation and never changes.
The final test set is used to train all five models.

challenges.hint: Each partition gets a turn as held-out validation data.

solution.code: Each fold is used once for validation while the other four are used for training.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: The process trains five models, holding out a different fold each time.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The final test set can remain separate for an evaluation after model selection.

challenges.title: Cost of missed fraud
challenges.description: For a fraud review system, missed fraudulent transactions are especially costly. Which additional metric directly measures the fraction of actual frauds detected?

choices.text: The number of input columns.
Recall for the fraud class.
Accuracy alone.
Mean absolute error on transaction amounts.

challenges.hint: Focus on actual fraud cases, including those the model misses.

solution.code: Recall for the fraud class.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Fraud recall is detected frauds divided by all actual frauds.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Precision and review capacity also matter, but accuracy alone can hide missed fraud in imbalanced data.

challenges.title: Starting a project
challenges.description: Before trying complex models for a new prediction task, why establish a simple baseline?

choices.text: It removes the need for a held-out evaluation.
It proves the data contains no errors.
It gives a reference for judging whether later models improve the task.
It guarantees that every complex model will perform worse.

challenges.hint: You need a meaningful point of comparison.

solution.code: It gives a reference for judging whether later models improve the task.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: A baseline makes it possible to measure the benefit of later changes.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Even a strong model still needs data checks and an appropriate evaluation.

challenges.title: Reading a residual
challenges.description: A model predicts 32 minutes; actual delivery takes 38 minutes. If residual = actual minus predicted, what is the residual?

choices.text: 6 minutes
-6 minutes
32 minutes
70 minutes

challenges.hint: Subtract the estimate from the observed value.

solution.code: 6 minutes

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Use the stated convention: observed minus predicted.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: 38 - 32 = 6, so the residual is positive 6 minutes; actual time exceeded the estimate.

challenges.title: Spotting a curved pattern
challenges.description: A model predicts energy use from temperature. Residuals are positive at low and high temperatures but negative in the middle. What should the analyst investigate?

choices.text: Whether training accuracy proves every prediction is correct.
Whether the target must become three class labels.
Whether residuals prove temperature causes energy use.
Whether a straight-line relationship misses a curved pattern.

challenges.hint: Look at how errors change across the input values.

solution.code: Whether a straight-line relationship misses a curved pattern.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The residuals change direction systematically instead of appearing random.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A curve in residuals suggests the linear form may miss structure; it does not prove causation.

challenges.title: Interpreting a slope
challenges.description: A rent model has an area coefficient of 20 dollars per month per square meter. What does it mean in the fitted model?

choices.text: The model is correct for 20 percent of apartments.
An apartment of 20 square meters must rent for 20 dollars.
Predicted monthly rent changes by 20 dollars per added square meter, with other inputs fixed.
Every apartment rent is exactly 20 dollars.

challenges.hint: Relate the coefficient to one unit of the feature.

solution.code: Predicted monthly rent changes by 20 dollars per added square meter, with other inputs fixed.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The coefficient describes how the model output changes when area rises by one square meter.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Its units are rent per area; it is not the whole rent or a guarantee for one apartment.

challenges.title: Interpreting an intercept
challenges.description: A model estimates child height from age, and its intercept is its predicted height at age zero. How should this value be treated?

choices.text: As proof that age has no relationship with height.
As the model estimate at age zero, which may not be meaningful for the intended age range.
As the average height of all children.
As the error for the oldest child.

challenges.hint: An intercept is the output when input terms are zero.

solution.code: As the model estimate at age zero, which may not be meaningful for the intended age range.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Check whether zero is realistic and relevant to the data.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: The value has a mathematical meaning at age zero but is not automatically a useful real-world summary.

challenges.title: Predicting beyond the data
challenges.description: A rent model saw apartments from 20 to 120 square meters. What is the main concern with predicting rent for a 500-square-meter apartment?

choices.text: The input is far outside the training range, so the estimate may be unreliable.
A linear model cannot calculate any number above 120.
A numeric input guarantees the estimate is accurate.
The model automatically gathers new examples first.

challenges.hint: Compare the request with the range the model has seen.

solution.code: The input is far outside the training range, so the estimate may be unreliable.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Five hundred is far beyond the largest observed area.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: The model can extrapolate, but the training data do not show whether the pattern continues that far.

challenges.title: Comparing residual size
challenges.description: Two price predictions have residuals -$4,000 and +$9,000. Which prediction is closer to its actual price?

choices.text: The prediction with the +$9,000 residual.
Both are equally close because one error is negative.
Neither has an error because residuals can be negative.
The prediction with the -$4,000 residual.

challenges.hint: Compare absolute sizes, not signs.

solution.code: The prediction with the -$4,000 residual.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The sign gives direction; magnitude gives distance from the observed value.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Absolute errors are $4,000 and $9,000, so the first prediction is closer.

challenges.title: Choosing a logistic target
challenges.description: A model flags whether a payment is fraudulent or legitimate. How should this binary target be represented?

choices.text: As a different continuous dollar amount for each class.
As an unlabeled cluster assignment.
As one of two outcome classes for each labeled payment.
As the payment position in a table.

challenges.hint: Focus on the outcome the model must decide between.

solution.code: As one of two outcome classes for each labeled payment.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Fraudulent and legitimate are two possible categories.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: The class label is the target; payment amount may be an input, not the class itself.

challenges.title: Interpreting a probability
challenges.description: A logistic model assigns an application a default probability of 0.25. What does that output alone say?

choices.text: The model has a 25 percent chance of having been trained.
The model estimates a 0.25 probability of default under its fitted model.
The application definitely will default.
Exactly one quarter of this application will default.

challenges.hint: Distinguish a probability estimate from a certain outcome.

solution.code: The model estimates a 0.25 probability of default under its fitted model.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The value is an estimate about the outcome, not the observed outcome itself.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A probability expresses uncertainty; it does not dictate what will happen to this particular application.

challenges.title: Logistic regression for a numeric target
challenges.description: A team uses logistic regression to predict the exact number of minutes until a bus arrives. What is the mismatch?

choices.text: The target is a numeric amount, while logistic regression is used for class probabilities.
The target is a number, so logistic regression is required.
Arrival time is an unlabeled cluster.
A numeric target cannot be measured.

challenges.hint: Focus on whether the requested output is a class or a measured amount.

solution.code: The target is a numeric amount, while logistic regression is used for class probabilities.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The task asks for an exact time in minutes, not one of two categories.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A regression approach is suited to numeric amounts; logistic regression models class probabilities.

challenges.title: Ranking probability scores
challenges.description: A model estimates default probabilities of 0.20 for Alex and 0.70 for Blair. Which statement follows from these scores?

choices.text: Alex is certain to default and Blair is certain not to.
The model predicts that exactly 20 percent of Alex will default.
The two estimates prove that Blair will default.
The model assigns Blair the higher estimated default risk.

challenges.hint: Compare the two probability estimates without treating either as certainty.

solution.code: The model assigns Blair the higher estimated default risk.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: A score of 0.70 is greater than 0.20, so the model estimates higher risk for Blair.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Blair ranks higher by estimated risk, but neither score proves an individual outcome.

challenges.title: Input or target
challenges.description: A model predicts whether a customer will renew. Which is a possible input available before the outcome?

choices.text: The model's predicted renewal probability.
The model's final class decision.
The number of support calls before the renewal date.
Whether the customer actually renewed.

challenges.hint: Inputs must be available before the outcome being predicted.

solution.code: The number of support calls before the renewal date.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Past support-call count can be known before the renewal decision.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Renewal is the target; the score and final class are model outputs.

challenges.title: Testing a forecast
challenges.description: A team forecasts future weekly demand from past weeks. Which split best imitates use?

choices.text: Use actual test-week demand as a forecast input.
Test on the latest weeks and train on earlier weeks.
Randomly mix all weeks, including future weeks in training.
Train on latest weeks and test on earliest weeks.

challenges.hint: Arrange the split in the same time direction as prediction.

solution.code: Test on the latest weeks and train on earlier weeks.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: At forecast time, past outcomes are known but future ones are not.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A later holdout simulates forecasting; training on later periods can leak unavailable information.

challenges.title: Testing new customers
challenges.description: Rows contain many transactions per customer. The goal is performance on entirely new customers. What split helps?

choices.text: Keep each customer's rows together in training or test, not both.
Place transactions from every customer in both sets.
Assign alternating rows after sorting by price.
Copy each test label into training features.

challenges.hint: Ask whether test cases should be new rows or new people.

solution.code: Keep each customer's rows together in training or test, not both.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Rows from one person can share patterns, making a row-level split overly easy.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A customer-level split reduces overlap when the intended use is new customers.

challenges.title: Preserving a rare class
challenges.description: Only 2 percent of examples are positive. What can stratifying a train/test split help do?

choices.text: Make every positive prediction correct.
Make positives as common as negatives.
Remove the need for class-specific metrics.
Keep the positive-class proportion reasonably similar in both partitions.

challenges.hint: Consider whether both sets contain the uncommon class.

solution.code: Keep the positive-class proportion reasonably similar in both partitions.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Stratification attempts to preserve class proportions while dividing examples.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: It helps represent the rare class but does not rebalance data or guarantee accuracy.

challenges.title: Keeping comparisons repeatable
challenges.description: A team wants to compare two model versions fairly on the same dataset. What helps keep their evaluation cases consistent?

choices.text: Train each version on the test labels.
Change the test examples until one model scores higher.
Save and reuse the same train/test split when comparing the versions.
Create a fresh split for each version and assume the scores are directly comparable.

challenges.hint: Hold the evaluation examples steady while changing the model.

solution.code: Save and reuse the same train/test split when comparing the versions.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The same saved partition makes the comparison less affected by different example assignments.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Reusing a split supports a fairer comparison; the test data must still remain separate from fitting and tuning.

challenges.title: Checking duplicate rows
challenges.description: Why check for duplicate records before randomly splitting data?

choices.text: Removing duplicates always lowers accuracy.
Copies in both partitions can make test performance look better than on new records.
Duplicates guarantee independent test examples.
Duplicates automatically become valid new labels.

challenges.hint: Imagine the same example on both sides of the split.

solution.code: Copies in both partitions can make test performance look better than on new records.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The model could see one copy during training and be scored on another.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Cross-partition duplicates can make evaluation unrepresentative; first check and handle duplicates appropriately.

challenges.title: Test population coverage
challenges.description: A model will be used in several regions, but the test set includes one region only. What limitation follows?

choices.text: The test may not show performance in the unrepresented regions.
A model cannot be tested on one region.
The test proves performance is equal in every region.
The model must have learned each region as a target.

challenges.hint: Compare test examples with intended use.

solution.code: The test may not show performance in the unrepresented regions.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The evaluation data lack examples from some deployment regions.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Results from one region cannot establish performance in unrepresented regions.

challenges.title: Accuracy with a rare class
challenges.description: Of 1,000 cases, 10 are fraud. A model predicts no fraud and gets 990 cases correct. What is its accuracy?

choices.text: 10 percent.
1 percent.
0 percent.
99 percent.

challenges.hint: Divide correct predictions by all examples.

solution.code: 99 percent.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: There are 990 correct predictions among 1,000 cases.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: 990 / 1,000 is 0.99; the high accuracy still hides that every fraud was missed.

challenges.title: Precision in a review queue

challenges.title: Iterating after a first model

Choose a more complex model using only its training score.
Tune repeatedly on the final test set.

challenges.title: Adding representative training data
challenges.description: A model memorizes a small training set and performs poorly on new cases. What could additional diverse training examples provide?

choices.text: More examples of patterns the model should generalize to.
A guarantee that the model will never err.
A replacement for held-out evaluation.
A way to reveal test labels during fitting.

challenges.hint: Think about how varied examples can distinguish patterns from quirks.

solution.code: More examples of patterns the model should generalize to.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea

steps.title: Apply it to the example

challenges.title: Combining tree predictions
challenges.description: A team combines predictions from many decision trees instead of relying on one tree. What is a possible benefit?

The combined model is guaranteed perfect on new data.
Evaluation is no longer needed.
The combined result may depend less on peculiar splits from a single tree.

steps.title: Apply it to the example

challenges.title: Learning a mistaken label
challenges.description: A flexible model fits a few incorrect training labels. Why may that hurt performance?

choices.text: The model automatically detects every wrong label.
Noise changes row order but never predictions.
It can learn noise specific to those examples instead of a general pattern.
Incorrect labels always improve test performance.

steps.explanation: Memorizing label noise may reduce performance on correctly labeled unseen examples.

challenges.title: Summarizing fold scores
challenges.description: Five cross-validation scores are 0.78, 0.82, 0.80, 0.76, and 0.84. What is a simple overall summary?

choices.text: Only the first fold's training score.
The mean of the five validation scores.
The maximum score as a guaranteed future result.
The sum of all target labels.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Their mean summarizes results across folds; the spread also shows variation.

challenges.title: Cross-validation with a small dataset
challenges.description: A small dataset leaves few examples in a single validation split. What can cross-validation offer?

choices.text: Several rotated validation estimates using different subsets for training and validation.
New independent examples created from nothing.
A guarantee each estimate equals production performance.
Permission to train on final test labels.

challenges.hint: Consider how rotating the held-out portion uses the available examples.

solution.code: Several rotated validation estimates using different subsets for training and validation.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Different folds take turns being held out.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Cross-validation uses the dataset more fully for assessment but cannot create data or guarantee future performance.

challenges.title: Interpreting variation across folds
challenges.description: A model gets validation scores from 0.55 to 0.90 across cross-validation folds. What should the team notice?

choices.text: Every fold has exactly the same examples.
The highest score is guaranteed on future data.
The model has no prediction errors.
Its measured performance varies substantially across the held-out folds.

challenges.hint: Compare the lowest and highest fold results.

solution.code: Its measured performance varies substantially across the held-out folds.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A wide spread signals variability worth investigating, even if the average score looks acceptable.

challenges.title: Random folds for forecasts
challenges.description: A model predicts later daily demand from earlier days. Why can ordinary random folds mislead?

choices.text: Time order is irrelevant to forecasting.
Models cannot process dates as inputs.
A training fold can contain days later than its validation days.
Random folds guarantee a future-only test.

challenges.hint: Check whether training examples could occur after validation in real use.

solution.code: A training fold can contain days later than its validation days.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Random assignment can mix earlier and later periods.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A time-aware split better reflects forecasts, where later observations should not inform earlier predictions.

challenges.title: Shuffling an irrelevant row order
challenges.description: A dataset is sorted by customer name, but the names have no relation to the prediction task and each row is independent. A cross-validation routine assigns consecutive rows to folds. What can improve fold comparability?

choices.text: Sort the target labels and use row number as the prediction.
Shuffle the rows before assigning them to folds.
Keep the alphabetical blocks so every fold has the same customer names.
Use every row in both training and validation at the same time.

challenges.hint: The current row order reflects a sorting key unrelated to the task.

solution.code: Shuffle the rows before assigning them to folds.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Consecutive folds may otherwise contain systematically different portions of the sorted table.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Shuffling before fold assignment reduces this irrelevant ordering effect when examples are independent.

challenges.title: Defining success first
challenges.description: Before seeing model results, a team records which mistakes matter and which metric it will report. Why?

choices.text: The evaluation criterion is explicit before results can influence the choice.
The model is guaranteed to meet the criterion.
The model cannot make false predictions.
Data checks are no longer needed.

challenges.hint: Consider how a prechosen measure guides interpretation.

solution.code: The evaluation criterion is explicit before results can influence the choice.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The team can judge results against a stated goal rather than changing the goal afterward.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A predefined criterion improves discipline but cannot ensure the model reaches it.

challenges.title: A small baseline improvement
challenges.description: A complex model scores 0.81 and a simple baseline 0.80 on the same held-out metric. What is the careful conclusion?

choices.text: It is unquestionably better for every use.
The baseline proves there is no useful signal.
The difference guarantees better production results.
The complex model shows a small measured gain that needs context.

challenges.hint: Compare the size of the gain and where it was measured.

solution.code: The complex model shows a small measured gain that needs context.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The observed scores differ by only 0.01 on that metric and dataset.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: That is a small measured gain, not proof of a practically meaningful or universal improvement.

challenges.title: Investigating reported errors
challenges.description: A classifier has an acceptable overall score, but users say one kind of example is often wrong. What should the team do?

choices.text: Replace all wrong predictions with the majority class.
Report only the training score.
Review errors by relevant example types to find patterns hidden by the aggregate.
Ignore the reports because the overall score is acceptable.

challenges.hint: Break results into meaningful subsets or error types.

solution.code: Review errors by relevant example types to find patterns hidden by the aggregate.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: An aggregate can hide where errors are concentrated.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Error analysis guides investigation; the overall score alone cannot explain the reported failures.

challenges.title: Checking feature availability
challenges.description: Evaluation uses a feature recorded only after the outcome the model predicts. What is wrong?

choices.text: The metric must be a clustering score.
The evaluation uses information unavailable at prediction time.
The test set necessarily has too few rows.
A later-recorded feature is always a valid input.

challenges.hint: Compare each feature's time with the decision time.

solution.code: The evaluation uses information unavailable at prediction time.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: A real prediction cannot use future information.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A post-outcome feature leaks information and can make measured performance unrealistically high.

challenges.title: Checking what the label means
challenges.description: A project label records whether a customer was contacted, but the team wants to predict whether help is needed. What should it verify?

choices.text: Whether contact is a valid, reliable measure of needing help.
Whether labels are sorted alphabetically.
Whether a complex model can hide the difference.
Whether all customers have identical features.

challenges.hint: Check if the recorded outcome really represents the question.

solution.code: Whether contact is a valid, reliable measure of needing help.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: A contact event is not necessarily the same as a need for help.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A model learns its provided label; label validity must be assessed separately from score.

challenges.title: Reporting evaluation context
challenges.description: A report gives accuracy but omits which dataset and split produced it. What context is missing?

choices.text: The color of the report title.
Only model variable names.
The spreadsheet's input-column order.
How examples were selected and kept separate for evaluation.

challenges.hint: A score needs context to be interpreted and repeated.

solution.code: How examples were selected and kept separate for evaluation.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: The data and split help explain what the score measures.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Without its dataset and split, a metric can be misleading and hard to reproduce.

challenges.title: Checking a model after release
challenges.description: A model met its launch target last month. Why continue checking inputs and outcomes?

choices.text: Monitoring automatically fixes any performance drop.
Every new example should be added to training without review.
Data or use conditions may change, so old results may not describe current behavior.
A launch metric remains accurate forever.

challenges.hint: Consider whether future data must match evaluation data exactly.

solution.code: Data or use conditions may change, so old results may not describe current behavior.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Real-world conditions and input patterns can change over time.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Monitoring provides signals for investigation; updates still require validation.

challenges.title: Scoping a first project
challenges.description: A team wants to use AI to improve the whole company. What is a better first step?

choices.text: Promise to automate every company decision.
Choose one specific decision or outcome and define a useful result.
Select the most complicated model before defining the task.
Collect every data source without a question.

challenges.hint: Make the goal concrete enough to evaluate.

solution.code: Choose one specific decision or outcome and define a useful result.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: A narrow question clarifies needed examples, target, and success measure.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A bounded task is easier to assess than a broad promise to improve everything.

challenges.title: Finding target labels
challenges.description: A team wants to predict urgent support tickets, but records have no urgency labels. What early step is needed?

choices.text: Determine how reliable urgency labels can be defined or obtained.
Train a supervised classifier without target examples.
Use model predictions as verified historical labels.
Choose a metric before defining urgent.

challenges.hint: Supervised learning needs examples paired with the outcome.

solution.code: Determine how reliable urgency labels can be defined or obtained.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Without labels, the team cannot directly train or evaluate a supervised urgency model.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Agree on a meaningful label and collect trustworthy examples before model training.

challenges.title: Documenting data sources
challenges.description: A project combines customer records from two spreadsheets. What should be documented before interpreting the merged data?

choices.text: Only the font used in each spreadsheet.
A guarantee every row refers to a different person.
An invented target for unmatched records.
Where records came from and how matches and field meanings were determined.

challenges.hint: Consider what someone needs to understand the merged data.

solution.code: Where records came from and how matches and field meanings were determined.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Source and matching rules affect which records and values the table represents.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Documenting provenance and transformations helps identify limitations and reproduce the dataset.

challenges.title: Resolving unclear labels
challenges.description: Two reviewers disagree about whether support tickets count as urgent. What should a first ML project do before training?

choices.text: Replace disputed labels with the model's own predictions.
Keep conflicting labels without documenting the disagreement.
Agree on a clear urgency definition and review ambiguous labels consistently.
Train immediately and assume the model will resolve the disagreement.

challenges.hint: The model needs a consistent target to learn from.

solution.code: Agree on a clear urgency definition and review ambiguous labels consistently.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Different reviewers currently apply different meanings to the same target label.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: A shared labeling rule makes training examples more consistent; model complexity cannot repair an undefined target.

challenges.title: Recording an experiment
challenges.description: A teammate should repeat an initial ML experiment. Which practice helps most directly?

choices.text: Use a different metric each time without recording it.
Record data version, preparation steps, model settings, and evaluation method.
Keep only a screenshot of the best score.
Change data and settings without notes.

challenges.hint: Capture choices needed to reconstruct the experiment.

solution.code: Record data version, preparation steps, model settings, and evaluation method.

steps.title: Identify the relevant idea
steps.explanation: Reproduction depends on knowing the data and workflow.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Recording these details lets another person rerun and interpret the experiment.

challenges.title: Defining project success
challenges.description: A team wants to reduce late deliveries. Which is a useful success criterion?

choices.text: Improve a chosen late-delivery measure on appropriate held-out data.
Use the model with the most parameters.
Maximize training accuracy regardless of test results.
Use AI even if the late-delivery process does not improve.

challenges.hint: Connect the criterion to the goal and held-out evidence.

solution.code: Improve a chosen late-delivery measure on appropriate held-out data.

steps.explanation: A useful measure relates the model to late deliveries and is tested on data not used to fit it.

steps.title: Apply it to the example
steps.explanation: Model size and training score alone do not show whether the intended outcome improves.

challenges.title: Combining models
challenges.description: Several independently trained models make numerical predictions. What is one purpose of averaging their predictions?

To guarantee that every averaged prediction is correct.
To remove the need for validation data.
To make all models have identical errors.

solution.code: To reduce variance when their errors are not perfectly correlated.

steps.title: Work it out
steps.explanation: Averaging can cancel some individual errors when models differ.

steps.explanation: The benefit depends on the models and their errors; it is not guaranteed.

challenges.title: Choosing model settings
challenges.description: You are comparing tree depths. Which data should guide the choice before a final evaluation?

Training and validation data, keeping the final test set untouched.

Only the final test labels used as features.

steps.explanation: Validation performance can guide the choice of tree depth.

challenges.title: Selecting features in cross-validation

On the final test set before training.
Inside each training fold, before scoring its validation fold.

challenges.title: Underfitting or overfitting?

Perfect generalization.
Proof that the validation labels were leaked.

challenges.title: Interpreting probabilities
challenges.description: Among many cases assigned a predicted probability near 0.7, about 70% are positive. What does this suggest about those probabilities?

The model has proven a causal relationship.

challenges.title: Layers and activation
challenges.description: Why do neural networks commonly apply nonlinear activation functions between layers?

To allow the network to represent nonlinear relationships.
To guarantee zero training error.

steps.explanation: Nonlinear activations allow the network to learn functions beyond a single linear transformation.

steps.explanation: Multiple linear layers without nonlinearities can be combined into one linear transformation.

challenges.title: What backpropagation computes

Gradients of the loss with respect to the model's parameters.
The final test labels.

steps.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate parameter gradients.

steps.explanation: An optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters; backpropagation itself does not guarantee an optimum.

challenges.title: Layers in image models

A requirement that all images have labels for every edge.
A method for replacing the test set.
Hierarchical feature learning.

steps.explanation: The learned patterns still need evaluation for shortcuts and generalization.

challenges.title: Preparing text

Converting the sentence into image pixels only.
Assigning the final test label to each word.
Sorting the words alphabetically and discarding their identity.

steps.explanation: A tokenizer splits text into tokens and maps them to model vocabulary IDs.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: The particular tokenization method and vocabulary must match the model.

challenges.title: Background shortcuts

Whether it learned the background instead of the intended object.
Whether every future image will have that same background.
Whether training accuracy alone proves object recognition.

steps.explanation: The model may exploit the background because it predicts the training labels.

steps.title: Check the distinction
steps.explanation: Testing with varied backgrounds can help reveal this shortcut.

challenges.title: Evaluating a forecast
challenges.description: You want to predict next month's demand using past observations. Which split best respects the forecasting task?

Use the validation period's outcome as an input at forecast time.

challenges.title: A new user's recommendations

Use future clicks as if they were already known.
Discard all item information and wait for a perfect history.
Use available item content and the user's stated preferences.

steps.explanation: Content features and stated preferences can provide signals before interaction history exists.

steps.explanation: Their usefulness should be evaluated; they do not eliminate cold-start uncertainty.

challenges.title: A safer deployment

Disabling all production monitoring.

challenges.hint: Think about returning to a known earlier version.

challenges.title: Training and serving inputs

challenges.hint: Compare the input transformation at training and inference.

solution.code: Training-serving inconsistency can change predictions unexpectedly.

challenges.title: Feature attribution

steps.explanation: Attribution describes a model's dependence on inputs under a particular method.

challenges.title: When Averaging Adds Little

challenges.title: A Costly Ensemble

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: An ensemble is useful only when its practical benefit justifies its added complexity.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: The response-time limit makes latency part of success, so compare the marginal gain with that cost.

challenges.title: Why Boosting Adds Learners

Boosting, which adds learners sequentially to correct earlier errors.

solution.code: Boosting, which adds learners sequentially to correct earlier errors.

steps.explanation: The later learners are explicitly guided by earlier mistakes.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: That sequential correction is the key idea of boosting, unlike independent averaging.

challenges.title: Averaging Numeric Predictions

challenges.title: Verifying an Ensemble Gain

Whether it has more parameters than either individual model.
Whether its training score is perfect, regardless of held-out results.
Whether both models produce identical predictions on training examples.

challenges.hint: Look for evidence that reflects performance on data not used to fit the models.

solution.code: Whether it improves performance or reliability on held-out data enough to justify its cost.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Training performance alone cannot establish that the combination generalizes better.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A held-out comparison tests the intended benefit while the cost check accounts for added complexity.

challenges.title: Choosing Models to Combine
