Their disagreement guarantees that every combined prediction is correct.

challenges.hint: Ask whether disagreement is useful and measured, rather than assuming it is always good.

solution.code: Their different errors may allow one model to offset some mistakes made by the other.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Error diversity creates an opportunity for averaging to reduce some mistakes.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: The opportunity must still be checked on held-out data; disagreement alone is not a guarantee.

challenges.title: Isolate a Hyperparameter Change
challenges.description: A tuning run changes both tree depth and regularization strength, and validation performance improves. What can the team conclude?

choices.text: Increasing tree depth alone caused the improvement.
Stronger regularization alone caused the improvement.
The combined setting improved the validation score, but the run does not show which change caused the improvement.
The final test score would identify which setting caused it.

challenges.hint: Notice that two settings changed at the same time.

solution.code: The combined setting improved the validation score, but the run does not show which change caused the improvement.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Because both hyperparameters changed together, their individual effects cannot be separated from this result.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Compare controlled settings on validation data and keep the final test out of the search.

challenges.title: A Long Search on One Validation Set
challenges.description: A team tries thousands of settings and repeatedly selects whichever has the best score on one validation set. What is a key risk?

choices.text: The search automatically turns the validation set into new training examples.
More settings guarantee that the true best setting has been found without bias.
The final test score becomes more reliable each time it is checked.
The selected setting may fit quirks of that validation set rather than generalize.

challenges.hint: Think about how repeated selection uses the same comparison data.

solution.code: The selected setting may fit quirks of that validation set rather than generalize.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A large search can adapt to random variation in the validation scores.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Track the search process and keep the final test set untouched for an independent check.

challenges.title: Comparing Learning Rates
challenges.description: With the model and data fixed, what does changing a learning rate primarily change during training?

choices.text: The size of parameter updates made from the computed gradients.
The number of input features available to the model.
The labels assigned to the training examples.
The proportion of examples reserved for final testing.

challenges.hint: Separate an optimization setting from the dataset and model inputs.

solution.code: The size of parameter updates made from the computed gradients.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A learning rate controls how far an optimizer moves in response to a gradient.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Compare candidate rates using a consistent validation procedure; changing it does not relabel or repartition data.

challenges.title: Define Tuning Success First
challenges.description: Before starting a hyperparameter search, a team writes down the minimum validation improvement needed to justify deployment complexity. What is the main benefit?

choices.text: It guarantees that the chosen model will outperform on every future example.
It lets the team use final test results to revise the criterion repeatedly.
It makes the selection criterion explicit before the team sees the results.
It removes the need to compare against a baseline.

challenges.hint: Consider how a predeclared rule affects decisions after results are visible.

solution.code: It makes the selection criterion explicit before the team sees the results.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A success condition set in advance reduces ad hoc decisions driven by observed scores.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: It still requires a fair validation comparison and does not guarantee future performance.

challenges.title: A Search Without a Baseline
challenges.description: A tuned model is reported to achieve 84% accuracy. What additional comparison most directly helps decide whether the tuning effort was worthwhile?

choices.text: Compare the tuned model only with the highest-scoring training run.
Measure a simple baseline with the same evaluation split and metric.
Replace the validation labels with model predictions.
Compare its accuracy with an unrelated model measured on different data.

challenges.hint: A meaningful comparison changes the model, not the evaluation conditions.

solution.code: Measure a simple baseline with the same evaluation split and metric.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A score by itself gives no indication of the value added by tuning.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A baseline measured on the same split and metric provides a fair reference point.

challenges.title: Reproducing a Tuning Result
challenges.description: A colleague needs to reproduce the best run from a hyperparameter search. Which record is most useful?

choices.text: The final test labels copied into the training data.
Only the model's training accuracy, without its settings.
The selected hyperparameter values, validation procedure, and measured score.
A list of every feature name, with no information about the search.

challenges.hint: Record enough of the experiment to repeat the comparison.

solution.code: The selected hyperparameter values, validation procedure, and measured score.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The final result depends on both the chosen settings and the way candidates were evaluated.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Keeping the settings and validation procedure with the score makes the selected run interpretable and reproducible.

challenges.title: Two Nearly Duplicate Features
challenges.description: A dataset contains both temperature in Celsius and the same temperature converted to Fahrenheit. What is a reasonable feature-selection consideration?

choices.text: One may be removed because it duplicates information already present in the other.
Keep both because duplicated measurements always double useful information.
Keep only the Fahrenheit value because feature selection must use that scale.
Remove both because correlated features cannot be used by any model.

challenges.hint: Ask whether both columns contribute distinct information to the task.

solution.code: One may be removed because it duplicates information already present in the other.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The conversion is deterministic, so the two columns carry the same underlying measurement.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Removing one can simplify the input without discarding distinct information; validate the resulting model.

challenges.title: A Feature That Adds Noise
challenges.description: A candidate input is unrelated to the target in the training data and does not improve held-out performance. What is a plausible reason to exclude it?

choices.text: It must be retained because every available column improves generalization.
It should be converted into the target label.
It adds complexity without demonstrated predictive value.
It proves the model needs a larger neural network.

challenges.hint: Focus on whether the input contributes reliable information.

solution.code: It adds complexity without demonstrated predictive value.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A noisy or irrelevant feature can add work and make the model harder to interpret.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: No held-out gain supports leaving it out, while the decision should be checked on suitable data.

challenges.title: A High-Ranking Proxy Feature
challenges.description: A feature-selection report ranks postal code highly, and the team knows postal code may correlate with a sensitive attribute. What should the team do next?

choices.text: Keep it automatically because high predictive ranking proves it is harmless.
Investigate the feature's proxy relationship and its effects across relevant groups.
Replace group evaluation with the overall accuracy score.
Treat the feature ranking as evidence that postal code causes the outcome.

challenges.hint: Predictive usefulness is not the only consideration for a selected input.

solution.code: Investigate the feature's proxy relationship and its effects across relevant groups.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A feature can carry information about a sensitive attribute indirectly.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Reviewing proxy effects and subgroup outcomes is needed before deciding whether its use is appropriate.

challenges.title: A Feature Arriving After Prediction
challenges.description: A model is meant to predict whether a shipment will be late at dispatch time. A candidate feature records the actual delivery date. What is the key issue?

choices.text: It is safe because any column correlated with lateness is available at dispatch.
It should be kept because delivery date is a model hyperparameter.
It is a valid feature as long as it is removed from the training labels.
The value is unavailable at prediction time and leaks future information.

challenges.hint: Check the timeline of when the value becomes known.

solution.code: The value is unavailable at prediction time and leaks future information.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The actual delivery date is recorded only after the prediction point.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A feature unavailable at dispatch cannot support a real dispatch-time prediction and can inflate evaluation results.

challenges.title: Selection Changes Across Folds
challenges.description: Different cross-validation folds select different members of a group of strongly correlated measurements, while predictive scores stay similar. What is a reasonable interpretation?

choices.text: Several correlated features may be interchangeable for prediction, so individual selections are unstable.
Every fold has discovered a different causal driver of the outcome.
The feature-selection procedure has guaranteed equal performance for all future data.
The features selected most often must be the only valid measurements.

challenges.hint: Compare the relationship among the candidate inputs, not only their individual ranks.

solution.code: Several correlated features may be interchangeable for prediction, so individual selections are unstable.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Correlated variables can provide similar information, allowing a selector to choose substitutes in different folds.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Report selection stability and predictive performance rather than treating one fold's choice as definitive.

challenges.title: Removing a Costly Measurement
challenges.description: A feature requires an expensive lab measurement for every prediction. Removing it does not reduce held-out performance. What is a direct benefit of excluding it?

choices.text: The model becomes guaranteed to be causal.
The system can avoid the measurement cost for future predictions.
The remaining features become independent of one another.
The final test labels become available earlier.

challenges.hint: Consider what must be collected when the model is used.

solution.code: The system can avoid the measurement cost for future predictions.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The feature has no measured held-out benefit but adds a cost at prediction time.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Removing it can simplify data collection, while held-out evaluation checks that model performance remains acceptable.

challenges.title: Strong Training Score, Weak Validation Score
challenges.description: A model has very low training error but much higher validation error. Which pattern is most consistent with this result?

choices.text: The model is necessarily underfitting both datasets.
The model may be overfitting training-specific patterns.
The model has proven that the validation labels are incorrect.
The model has zero variance because its training error is low.

challenges.hint: Compare how well the model fits the examples it learned from and unseen examples.

solution.code: The model may be overfitting training-specific patterns.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A large gap between training and validation performance is a common sign of overfitting.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: The gap suggests the fitted patterns may not generalize; the scores do not prove the validation labels are wrong.

challenges.title: Finding a Useful Complexity Range
challenges.description: Validation error falls as tree depth increases, then rises for deeper trees. What does the rising portion suggest?

choices.text: Increasing depth has made the model simpler and increased its bias.
The final test set should be used to select the exact depth.
Training error must have risen by exactly the same amount.
Additional complexity is beginning to fit patterns that do not generalize well.

challenges.hint: Look at the direction of validation performance as complexity grows.

solution.code: Additional complexity is beginning to fit patterns that do not generalize well.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The validation score initially benefits from added capacity but eventually worsens.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: That later rise is consistent with increasing variance or overfitting, so choose using validation rather than the test set.

challenges.title: Reducing a Train-Validation Gap
challenges.description: A flexible model fits training data very closely but performs worse on validation data. Which experiment can test whether limiting complexity helps?

choices.text: Increase regularization and compare both training and validation performance.
Remove all validation examples and report the training score.
Increase complexity without measuring validation performance.
Tune directly against the final test labels.

challenges.hint: Choose an experiment that constrains how closely the model can follow training details.

solution.code: Increase regularization and compare both training and validation performance.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Regularization discourages overly complex fits and can reduce sensitivity to training noise.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Check whether validation performance improves; training error may increase as regularization strengthens.

challenges.title: When More Examples May Help
challenges.description: A complex model performs well on training data but inconsistently across different training samples. Which change may help reduce this instability?

choices.text: Increasing model complexity further without more evaluation.
Removing all examples that the model predicts correctly.
Collecting more representative training examples.
Selecting the model using the final test set.

challenges.hint: Consider what would make the fitted model less dependent on one sample.

solution.code: Collecting more representative training examples.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: High variance means the learned result changes substantially with the training sample.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: More representative data can stabilize learning, though the effect should be verified with held-out evaluation.

challenges.title: Low and Similar Errors
challenges.description: A model has low training and validation error, and the two values are close across several splits. What is the most supported conclusion?

choices.text: The model is overfitting because both error values are low.
The model is underfitting because the two error values are close.
These results show a good fit on the measured data, with no obvious high-bias or high-variance pattern.
The model is guaranteed to perform perfectly on future data.

challenges.hint: Consider both the error level and the gap between the two results.

solution.code: These results show a good fit on the measured data, with no obvious high-bias or high-variance pattern.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Low errors indicate a good fit on these samples, while their small gap gives no obvious sign of high variance.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: This is evidence about the evaluated data, not a guarantee about every future dataset.

challenges.title: What Learning Curves Can Show
challenges.description: A team plots training and validation error as the number of training examples grows. What can these curves help diagnose?

choices.text: Whether a model's predictions are automatically causal.
Which final test labels should be changed.
Whether the test set can be reused for hyperparameter search.
Whether performance patterns are consistent with underfitting or overfitting as data grows.

challenges.hint: Think about what comparisons across training sizes reveal.

solution.code: Whether performance patterns are consistent with underfitting or overfitting as data grows.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The two curves show how fit on seen and unseen examples changes with more data.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Their gap and level can inform a bias-variance diagnosis, but they do not prove causality or replace a held-out test.

challenges.title: A Costly Missed Positive
challenges.description: A screening system has false negatives that are much more costly than reviewing extra false positives. How should the team choose its decision threshold?

choices.text: Always use a threshold of 0.5 because costs cannot affect it.
Choose the threshold that maximizes training accuracy regardless of costs.
Use validation data to compare thresholds under the stated error costs.
Choose the threshold after inspecting final test outcomes repeatedly.

challenges.hint: Translate the operational consequences into a comparison rule.

solution.code: Use validation data to compare thresholds under the stated error costs.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The preferred threshold depends on the relative costs of the two error types.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Evaluating candidate thresholds on validation data using those costs aligns the decision with the stated goal.

challenges.title: Effect of Lowering a Positive Threshold
challenges.description: A binary classifier labels a case positive when its score meets a threshold. If the threshold is lowered, what is the usual tradeoff?

choices.text: Fewer cases are labeled positive, so recall must fall and false positives disappear.
More cases are labeled positive, often raising recall while also risking more false positives.
Every predicted probability becomes better calibrated.
The ranking of all model scores is necessarily reversed.

challenges.hint: Track how many cases cross the decision boundary in each direction.

solution.code: More cases are labeled positive, often raising recall while also risking more false positives.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Lowering the cutoff makes it easier for a case to receive a positive label.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: This can capture additional true positives but may also admit more false positives; the actual balance depends on the data.

challenges.title: Overall Score Hides a Group Difference
challenges.description: A model has strong overall accuracy, but the team suspects it performs differently across age groups. What should it report?

choices.text: Only the single overall accuracy because subgroup results cannot be informative.
Only the training loss for the largest group.
A separate decision threshold for each person without evaluating outcomes.
Relevant performance metrics for each age group as well as overall results.

challenges.hint: Check whether an aggregate metric masks different group outcomes.

solution.code: Relevant performance metrics for each age group as well as overall results.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Overall results can conceal variation across subgroups.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Comparing subgroup metrics helps reveal disparities that an overall score alone would miss.

challenges.title: A Fixed Review Capacity
challenges.description: A team can manually review only 40 cases per day. Each case has a risk score, and the team wants to use its capacity on the highest-risk cases. What rule fits this constraint?

choices.text: Flag every case above 0.5, even if that exceeds the review limit.
Rank cases by score and send the 40 highest-scoring cases for review.
Choose the 40 lowest-scoring cases for review.
Use final test labels to select cases after deployment.

challenges.hint: Use the scores to prioritize cases while respecting the fixed capacity.

solution.code: Rank cases by score and send the 40 highest-scoring cases for review.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The number of reviews is capped, so ordering cases by risk directly matches the constraint.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Selecting the top 40 uses available capacity without requiring a fixed probability cutoff.

challenges.title: Evaluating a Rare Positive Class
challenges.description: In a dataset where positive cases are rare, why might a team inspect precision and recall in addition to overall accuracy?

choices.text: Precision and recall are unaffected by the number of errors.
Accuracy directly measures whether predicted probabilities are calibrated.
Accuracy can look high even when a model misses many positives or produces many false alarms.
A rare class makes every negative prediction incorrect.

challenges.hint: Consider how many examples belong to each class and what errors are hidden by the total.

solution.code: Accuracy can look high even when a model misses many positives or produces many false alarms.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: With many negatives, predicting mostly negative can produce a high accuracy score.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Precision and recall make the positive-case tradeoff more visible for the intended task.

challenges.title: Calibration Can Differ by Group
challenges.description: A risk model is calibrated overall, but among one age group its predictions near 0.8 correspond to positive outcomes only about half the time. What should the team check?

choices.text: Calibration within that age group, rather than relying only on the overall result.
Whether the overall calibration score proves every group is calibrated.
Whether the model has more hidden layers than the training data.
Whether the final test labels can be added to model inputs.

challenges.hint: An overall average can hide group-specific probability errors.

solution.code: Calibration within that age group, rather than relying only on the overall result.

steps.title: Compare predicted and observed rates
steps.explanation: Predictions near 0.8 should correspond to outcomes around 80 percent in the population being checked; this group is closer to 50 percent.

steps.title: Inspect subgroups separately
steps.explanation: Overall calibration can hide miscalibration within a subgroup, so report group-level probability reliability.

challenges.title: Choosing a Metric for Deployment
challenges.description: A product team asks for "the best metric" before explaining what kinds of errors matter or how predictions will be used. What is the sound response?

choices.text: Use accuracy for every task because metrics are interchangeable.
Select the metric with the largest numeric value, regardless of scale.
Choose a metric only after seeing which one makes the model look strongest.
Clarify the decision context and error costs before choosing metrics.

challenges.hint: A measurement is useful only in relation to the intended decision.

solution.code: Clarify the decision context and error costs before choosing metrics.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Different metrics emphasize different aspects of prediction quality.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Operational assumptions and error consequences determine which measurements are relevant to report.

challenges.title: Role of a Hidden Layer
challenges.description: A neural network takes two numeric inputs, applies learned weights in a hidden layer, and passes the result onward. What is the hidden layer doing?

choices.text: Replacing the training labels with new input features.
Transforming the input into a learned intermediate representation.
Guaranteeing that the network has learned the correct causal model.
Selecting the final test examples for evaluation.

challenges.hint: Focus on what learned weights do between the input and output.

solution.code: Transforming the input into a learned intermediate representation.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A hidden layer computes intermediate values from the input using learned parameters.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Those values form a representation that later layers can use to make a task prediction.

challenges.title: What Network Weights Represent
challenges.description: A network starts with weights that do not yet make useful predictions. During training, what should happen to those weights?

choices.text: They are replaced by the validation labels after each prediction.
They are fixed permanently because neural networks do not learn parameters.
They become a list of all possible future inputs.
They are adjusted using training data so the model's predictions fit the learning objective better.

challenges.hint: Distinguish learned parameters from examples and labels.

solution.code: They are adjusted using training data so the model's predictions fit the learning objective better.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Weights are model parameters that determine how layer values are computed.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Training updates them to improve the objective, while separate evaluation checks whether that improvement generalizes.

challenges.title: Choosing a Deeper Network
challenges.description: A team considers adding several layers to a small dataset, but the current simpler model already meets the quality target. What is the best consideration?

choices.text: Compare the deeper model's expected benefit with its data and compute needs.
Add layers automatically because depth always improves accuracy.
Discard the simpler model because only deep networks can learn patterns.
Stop measuring performance once the deeper model begins training.

challenges.hint: More model capacity comes with practical costs and is not a guaranteed improvement.

solution.code: Compare the deeper model's expected benefit with its data and compute needs.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The course notes that extra layers do not ensure better results.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A measured comparison should include held-out quality, data sufficiency, and compute cost.

challenges.title: Architecture Setting or Learned Weight
challenges.description: A team chooses the number of hidden layers before training, while the network adjusts connection weights during training. Which is a hyperparameter?

choices.text: The number of hidden layers.
The learned value of a connection weight.
A particular training example.
The prediction made for one input.

challenges.hint: Separate design choices made before fitting from values learned during fitting.

solution.code: The number of hidden layers.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The team sets the layer count as part of the network design.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Connection weights are learned from data, whereas layer count is a chosen architecture setting.

challenges.title: Testing Whether a Network Is Needed
challenges.description: A team proposes a neural network for a small tabular task but has not tested a simpler model. What is a useful first step?

choices.text: Assume a neural network must outperform simpler models on every dataset.
Skip evaluation because neural networks learn features automatically.
Measure a simple baseline before deciding whether the network adds value.
Tune the network on the final test set before training a baseline.

challenges.hint: A baseline provides context for the added complexity.

solution.code: Measure a simple baseline before deciding whether the network adds value.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A neural model can require more compute and data without improving the result.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A comparable baseline shows whether that extra effort yields a useful held-out gain.

challenges.title: Why Stack Learned Layers
challenges.description: A later layer combines outputs from earlier layers rather than receiving only the original raw input. What does this allow the network to do?

choices.text: Build more useful representations from intermediate features.
Make every intermediate value a ground-truth label.
Avoid using training data to set its parameters.
Guarantee that the learned representation works under every distribution shift.

challenges.hint: Think about how successive transformations can reuse earlier results.

solution.code: Build more useful representations from intermediate features.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Each layer can transform what the preceding layer has already represented.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: This supports richer learned representations, but generalization still needs evaluation.

challenges.title: Gradients Through Several Layers
challenges.description: A loss depends on the output of a network, which depends on multiple earlier layers. How does backpropagation find gradients for an early layer's parameters?

choices.text: It compares the early parameters with final test labels directly.
It tries every possible parameter value and keeps the best one.
It copies the output gradient unchanged without accounting for earlier layers.
It applies the chain rule through the sequence of layer computations.

challenges.hint: Trace how a change in an early parameter can affect the final loss.

solution.code: It applies the chain rule through the sequence of layer computations.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The loss depends on the early parameter through the computations in later layers.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: The chain rule combines these dependencies to calculate the gradient efficiently.

challenges.title: Backpropagation and Parameter Updates
challenges.description: During training, backpropagation has computed parameter gradients. What is the optimizer's role next?

choices.text: Create additional labeled examples from the validation set.
Use the gradients to update the parameters according to an update rule.
Choose which metric the product should optimize without input from the team.
Guarantee that the model has reached a global optimum.

challenges.hint: Separate calculating the gradient from acting on it.

solution.code: Use the gradients to update the parameters according to an update rule.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Backpropagation provides information about how the loss changes with parameters.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: An optimizer uses that information to make updates, but those updates do not guarantee a global optimum.

challenges.title: What a Gradient Tells You
challenges.description: A parameter's loss gradient is positive at its current value. What does that say locally?

choices.text: Increasing that parameter slightly would increase the loss, holding other local conditions fixed.
The parameter is irrelevant to the loss at every possible value.
The model has found the global minimum.
The learning rate is necessarily too large.

challenges.hint: Interpret the sign as a local slope, not a complete training diagnosis.

solution.code: Increasing that parameter slightly would increase the loss, holding other local conditions fixed.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A positive derivative means the loss rises locally as that parameter increases.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: An optimizer may move against the gradient when minimizing loss, but the derivative alone does not set the learning rate or prove an optimum.

challenges.title: Gradient Does Not Choose Step Size
challenges.description: A training run computes sensible gradients, but parameter updates oscillate and loss fails to settle. What should the team consider?

choices.text: Whether backpropagation should be replaced with final test labels.
Whether every input feature should be removed.
Whether the learning rate or other optimization settings make updates too large.
Whether a gradient guarantees that the model architecture is appropriate.

challenges.hint: The gradient and the size of an update are related but distinct.

solution.code: Whether the learning rate or other optimization settings make updates too large.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Gradients indicate local loss direction with respect to parameters.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A learning rate controls update magnitude, so it can cause unstable steps even when gradients are computed correctly.

challenges.title: A Zero Gradient at One Point
challenges.description: The gradient of the loss with respect to one parameter is zero at its current value. What can be concluded from that fact alone?

choices.text: The model has definitely reached the global minimum.
The parameter has no effect on the loss at any possible value.
The network no longer needs evaluation data.
The loss has a locally flat slope for that parameter at the current point; it is not proof of a global minimum.

challenges.hint: Interpret the derivative at the current point, not at every possible setting.

solution.code: The loss has a locally flat slope for that parameter at the current point; it is not proof of a global minimum.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A zero derivative indicates no local first-order change in the loss along that parameter at this point.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Other points may have lower loss, so this alone does not establish a global optimum.

challenges.title: Representation Learning Still Needs Data
challenges.description: A deep model is trained on medical images whose diagnoses were assigned inconsistently. What should the team address before simply adding more layers?

choices.text: Review and improve label quality, then evaluate the model on representative held-out images.
Add layers because a deeper network automatically corrects inconsistent labels.
Use the final test labels as inputs during training.
Ignore the labels and compare only training accuracy.

challenges.hint: A model learns from the examples and targets it is given.

solution.code: Review and improve label quality, then evaluate the model on representative held-out images.

steps.title: Check the learning signal
steps.explanation: Inconsistent diagnoses give the model an unreliable target to learn from.

steps.title: Validate the revised data
steps.explanation: Improving labels and checking representative held-out examples addresses data quality more directly than adding model depth.

challenges.title: Deep Learning for Speech
challenges.description: A speech team wants a multilayer model to learn useful patterns from audio examples instead of manually specifying every representation. Which broad approach matches this goal?

choices.text: Feature selection, which only removes input columns.
Deep learning, which uses multilayer networks to learn representations from data.
A recommendation system, which ranks items from user interactions.
A data pipeline, which validates and transforms incoming records.

challenges.hint: Focus on the method that learns layered representations from examples.

solution.code: Deep learning, which uses multilayer networks to learn representations from data.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The team wants representations to be learned by a multilayer model.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: That is the broad role of deep learning in tasks such as speech, text, and vision.

challenges.title: Deep Model Versus Simpler Alternative
challenges.description: A deep network takes much longer to train than a small baseline, while their validation scores are similar. What is the best conclusion?

choices.text: The deep network must be chosen because it has more layers.
Validation scores should be ignored whenever training takes longer.
The baseline should be rejected because it cannot learn any patterns.
The extra depth has not yet shown a benefit that justifies its added cost.

challenges.hint: Compare measured performance with the compute required.

solution.code: The extra depth has not yet shown a benefit that justifies its added cost.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A multi-layer model can require more resources without improving results.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Similar validation scores provide no evidence that the extra compute is currently worthwhile.

challenges.title: A Learned Pattern Fails in a New Setting
challenges.description: A deep model performs well on one hospital's images but poorly on images from a different hospital. What is the most useful interpretation?

choices.text: Its training score proves that the new hospital's labels are wrong.
Its learned representations may not generalize to the changed data setting.
Adding layers guarantees performance will recover without new evaluation.
The model no longer needs regularization or data checks.

challenges.hint: Compare the new data with the setting used during training.

solution.code: Its learned representations may not generalize to the changed data setting.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Good results on one source do not guarantee performance under a changed distribution.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Evaluate representative data from the new setting and investigate differences before relying on the model.

challenges.title: Detecting Serving Failures
challenges.description: A deployed prediction API starts returning failed requests even though the model passed offline evaluation. Which production signal should the team monitor to detect this failure?

choices.text: Only the model training accuracy saved before deployment.
The number of layers in the trained model.
The API request error rate and service availability.
The average value of the training labels.

challenges.hint: Check whether requests are being served successfully.

solution.code: The API request error rate and service availability.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Offline model scores do not reveal whether the live service is returning successful responses.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Request failures and availability measure serving health and can trigger investigation or rollback.

challenges.title: Classifying Support Messages
challenges.description: A system assigns each incoming support message to a topic such as billing, delivery, or account access. Which NLP task is this?

choices.text: Machine translation.
Text classification.
Image segmentation.
Time-series forecasting.

challenges.hint: Identify whether the output is a category, translated text, or extracted field.

solution.code: Text classification.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The system maps a whole message to one of a set of topic labels.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Assigning a label to text is a classification task.

challenges.title: Extracting Dates from Messages
challenges.description: A system reads a customer message and returns the date mentioned in it as a structured field. Which task best describes this?

choices.text: Collaborative filtering.
Image classification.
Information extraction from text.
Probability calibration.

challenges.hint: Focus on turning part of the text into a structured value.

solution.code: Information extraction from text.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The system is locating a specific piece of information within the message.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Extracting a date into a field is information extraction, not assigning a topic label.

challenges.title: Choosing an NLP Task for Translation
challenges.description: A tool receives a sentence in Spanish and outputs the same meaning in English. Which NLP task is being performed?

choices.text: Text classification.
Feature selection.
Image recognition.
Machine translation.

challenges.hint: Compare the input and output types.

solution.code: Machine translation.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The system produces a sentence in a different language.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Converting text from one language to another while preserving meaning is translation.

challenges.title: Rare Words and Tokenization
challenges.description: A text model handles common words well but splits an uncommon product name into several pieces. What should the team investigate?

choices.text: Whether the tokenizer's vocabulary and tokenization choices suit the text.
Whether the model should sort all tokens alphabetically.
Whether the uncommon name should be used as the final test label.
Whether every rare word must be represented by one unique token.

challenges.hint: The conversion from raw text to model units can affect rare terms.

solution.code: Whether the tokenizer's vocabulary and tokenization choices suit the text.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Tokenizers divide text into units based on their rules and vocabulary.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Inspecting those choices can explain how an uncommon name is represented without requiring one token per word.

challenges.title: Producing a Draft Reply
challenges.description: A language system takes a user prompt and produces a new sentence as its output. Which broad NLP task does this most closely represent?

choices.text: Text classification.
Feature selection.
Text generation.
Time-series decomposition.

challenges.hint: Look at whether the output is a new piece of language or a label.

solution.code: Text generation.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The system is producing text rather than choosing a fixed category.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Generating a draft sentence is a text-generation task.

challenges.title: Preserving Negation in Text
challenges.description: A text classifier gives nearly identical results for "I liked the service" and "I did not like the service." What preprocessing detail should the team inspect first?

choices.text: Whether the word "not" is preserved and represented in the input text.
Whether the sentence is converted into image pixels.
Whether the user-item interaction table contains the sentence.
Whether the model is evaluated with a time-series split.

challenges.hint: Look for a short word that reverses the sentence meaning.

solution.code: Whether the word "not" is preserved and represented in the input text.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The two sentences differ by a negation word.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: If preprocessing drops or mishandles "not," the model may receive inputs that appear much more similar than their meanings.

challenges.title: What a Convolutional Filter Detects
challenges.description: A small filter moves across neighboring pixels in an image and responds strongly to a particular local pattern. What can it detect?

choices.text: The exact future label for every image.
A user's item preferences from interaction history.
Whether the image's filename is alphabetically first.
A local visual feature such as an edge or texture.

challenges.hint: Focus on the pattern within nearby pixels.

solution.code: A local visual feature such as an edge or texture.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A spatial filter examines local neighborhoods as it moves across the image.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Its responses can indicate local structures such as edges or textures.

challenges.title: A Camera Change Hurts Accuracy
challenges.description: An image classifier works on one camera but makes more errors on another camera's images. What is a useful evaluation step?

choices.text: Use only the original camera's training score as proof of robustness.
Test on images from the second camera and other relevant environments.
Assume that spatial filters make camera differences irrelevant.
Remove all images from the second camera before measuring performance.

challenges.hint: Evaluation data should reflect the settings where predictions will be used.

solution.code: Test on images from the second camera and other relevant environments.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Camera and environment changes can alter image patterns.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Measuring representative images from those settings reveals whether performance transfers.

challenges.title: Ranking Recommendation Candidates
challenges.description: A service estimates how relevant several products are to a user and must present the best matches first. What is the recommender expected to produce?

choices.text: A ranked list of candidate items ordered by predicted relevance.
A chronological split of training and test dates.
A set of pixel-level edge labels for each product.
A guarantee that every user will click the first item.

challenges.hint: Focus on the order in which the candidates should be presented.

solution.code: A ranked list of candidate items ordered by predicted relevance.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The system estimates how relevant candidate items are to the user.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Sorting candidates by predicted relevance gives the requested recommendation ranking.

challenges.title: Why Image Neighborhoods Matter
challenges.description: A convolutional filter is applied to an image whose pixels have been randomly shuffled across locations. Which capability is most directly disrupted?

choices.text: Recognizing whether the image file is in a folder.
Using the correct class names in the output report.
Counting how many training examples were collected.
Detecting local spatial patterns such as edges and textures.

challenges.hint: Consider what information a small filter gets from nearby pixels.

solution.code: Detecting local spatial patterns such as edges and textures.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A convolutional filter examines neighborhoods in the image.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Shuffling pixel locations destroys neighborhood structure, making local patterns harder to detect.

challenges.title: Inconsistent Image Labels
challenges.description: Two visually identical images receive different labels in the training data. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the model needs twice as many convolutional filters.
Whether image resolution can determine the correct label by itself.
Whether the validation set should be included as training data before scoring.
Whether labeling rules were applied consistently.

challenges.hint: Separate a data-label problem from a model-capacity problem.

solution.code: Whether labeling rules were applied consistently.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Conflicting labels for equivalent examples make the learning target unclear.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Review the labeling criteria and examples before attributing the issue to the vision architecture.

challenges.title: Local Filter and Whole Image
challenges.description: Why can repeatedly applying local filters be useful in image processing?

choices.text: It can detect similar local patterns at different image locations.
It guarantees that all scenes have identical backgrounds.
It removes the need to evaluate the model on new images.
It assigns a causal explanation to each pixel.

challenges.hint: Think about what happens as a filter is applied across the image.

solution.code: It can detect similar local patterns at different image locations.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A moving filter examines neighborhoods in multiple parts of the image.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: This lets it respond to a local feature wherever that feature appears.

challenges.title: Predicting with a Lag
challenges.description: A shop forecasts tomorrow's demand using the demand observed today. In a time-series feature table, today's observed demand is best described as what?

choices.text: A future target that is already known at prediction time.
A random validation label.
A lagged value used as an input for the next forecast.
A model's learning rate.

challenges.hint: Check the relative time of the observation and forecast.

solution.code: A lagged value used as an input for the next forecast.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Today's value is earlier than tomorrow's prediction.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: It can serve as a lag feature if it is available when the forecast is made.

challenges.title: Recognizing Weekly Seasonality
challenges.description: A cafe sees demand rise every Saturday and fall every Monday across many weeks. What kind of pattern is this?

choices.text: A one-time data-pipeline failure.
A recurring weekly seasonal pattern.
A random hyperparameter setting.
A guarantee that demand will rise every calendar day.

challenges.hint: Look for a pattern that repeats at a regular calendar interval.

solution.code: A recurring weekly seasonal pattern.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The same weekday pattern appears over multiple weeks.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A repeating weekly cycle is seasonality and may be represented with calendar features.

challenges.title: Separating Trend from Seasonality
challenges.description: A product's demand grows gradually over several years, while also peaking each December. Which interpretation is best?

choices.text: The gradual rise is a trend, and the recurring December peak is seasonality.
Both patterns are random noise because they occur at different scales.
The December peak is a trend and the long-term rise is a one-day lag.
The two patterns prove that random splitting is appropriate.

challenges.hint: Distinguish a long-term direction from a repeating calendar cycle.

solution.code: The gradual rise is a trend, and the recurring December peak is seasonality.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Growth across years describes an overall direction in the series.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A recurring December peak is a seasonal pattern layered on that trend.

challenges.title: Forecasting Without Future Inputs
challenges.description: A forecast is made at the end of March for April demand. Which calendar feature can safely be used if it is known in advance?

choices.text: April's actual demand, collected after the month ends.
The number of returns recorded in May.
A label assigned after reviewing April's forecast errors.
The month identifier for April.

challenges.hint: Use values available at the time the forecast is issued.

solution.code: The month identifier for April.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The forecast date determines which inputs are known.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A future month's calendar identity is known beforehand, unlike its realized demand or later outcomes.

challenges.title: A Simple Seasonal Forecast
challenges.description: A retailer's demand is highly similar each week, with each weekday following a repeated pattern. What is a sensible baseline forecast for next Monday?

choices.text: Use demand from a future Tuesday that has not happened.
Use demand from a comparable recent Monday as a reference.
Shuffle all dates and average their labels as a forecast.
Use a randomly chosen model setting as the forecast value.

challenges.hint: Compare the target date with earlier dates at a similar seasonal position.

solution.code: Use demand from a comparable recent Monday as a reference.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Repeated weekday behavior makes a prior Monday a relevant reference.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: This simple seasonal baseline can be compared with more complex forecasting methods.

challenges.title: Representing a Gradual Trend
challenges.description: A store observes demand rising steadily over several months. Which feature could help a forecasting model represent this gradual change?

choices.text: A future month's observed demand added before it occurs.
A shuffled row number unrelated to date.
A fixed label copied from the final test period.
A time index or other feature representing the series trend.

challenges.hint: Look for an input that captures how the series changes over time.

solution.code: A time index or other feature representing the series trend.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A steady rise over months is a trend rather than a repeating seasonal cycle.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A time-related trend feature can represent the gradual direction without using future outcomes.

challenges.title: Similar Users, Similar Items
challenges.description: A recommendation system suggests books based on patterns in what users with similar reading histories enjoyed. Which signal is it primarily using?

choices.text: Collaborative interaction patterns.
Only the books' written descriptions, with no user activity.
A time-series trend in daily temperature.
A probability threshold selected for image classification.

challenges.hint: Identify whether the evidence comes from behavior or item attributes.

solution.code: Collaborative interaction patterns.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The recommendation relies on patterns across user-item interactions.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Using similarities in observed behavior is a collaborative signal.

challenges.title: Matching Known Interests to Item Content
challenges.description: A user who likes vegetarian recipes has rated several books. The service compares descriptions across its catalog to find similar titles. Which signal is it using?

choices.text: Match item content features with the user's known interests.
Use only similarities in clicks from users with the same history.
Use future ratings that have not yet been collected.
Use the number of hidden layers in an image classifier.

challenges.hint: Distinguish information about the items from patterns of user activity.

solution.code: Match item content features with the user's known interests.

steps.title: Identify the information source
steps.explanation: The book descriptions provide attributes about each item, and the user's previous likes provide a profile of interests.

steps.title: Apply the recommendation method
steps.explanation: Matching item attributes with known interests is a content-based signal, rather than a similarity derived only from other users' interactions.

challenges.title: Why Combine Recommendation Signals
challenges.description: A service has rich item descriptions and many user-item interactions. What does a hybrid recommender do?

choices.text: Uses only item descriptions and discards all interaction data.
Uses only interaction history and forbids item information.
Combines content information with collaborative interaction signals.
Combines unrelated model errors without checking relevance.

challenges.hint: Consider how two different sources of recommendation evidence can be used together.

solution.code: Combines content information with collaborative interaction signals.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Descriptions provide item-content information, while interactions reveal behavior patterns.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A hybrid method uses both sources to rank candidates.

challenges.title: Clicks Depend on Display Position
challenges.description: A highly ranked item receives more clicks after being moved to the first position, even though its content is unchanged. What should the team consider?

choices.text: The move proves that users prefer the item's content in all contexts.
Exposure and position may affect clicks, so clicks alone do not measure preference.
The item has become a new user profile.
Click counts are unaffected by where recommendations appear.

challenges.hint: Ask what changed besides the item itself.

solution.code: Exposure and position may affect clicks, so clicks alone do not measure preference.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The item received more prominent exposure after its position changed.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Observed clicks can reflect placement as well as underlying user preference.

challenges.title: Popularity and Recommendation Coverage
challenges.description: A recommender has good click-through on popular products but rarely shows items from the rest of the catalog. Which additional property should the team examine?

choices.text: Catalog coverage, to see how broadly recommendations include available items.
Only training accuracy, because coverage is a model parameter.
The number of layers in the recommendation network.
Whether all products can be assigned the same rating.

challenges.hint: Look beyond clicks on the most frequently shown items.

solution.code: Catalog coverage, to see how broadly recommendations include available items.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A system can perform well on popular items while neglecting much of the catalog.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Coverage measures whether recommendations span a useful range of items.

challenges.title: An Unseen Item Is Not a Dislike
challenges.description: A user has never been shown a particular movie, so the interaction table contains no rating or click for it. What can the system safely conclude from that absence alone?

choices.text: The user strongly dislikes the movie.
The user has already watched the movie.
Nothing definite about the user's preference; the item may simply not have been exposed.
The movie must be recommended to every user.

challenges.hint: Separate an unobserved interaction from an explicit negative response.

solution.code: Nothing definite about the user's preference; the item may simply not have been exposed.

steps.title: Check what was observed
steps.explanation: The interaction table has no record because the user was not shown the movie.

steps.title: Avoid inferring a preference
steps.explanation: An unobserved interaction is not evidence that the user disliked the item; exposure and position affect which clicks are observed.

challenges.title: Monitoring a Prediction API
challenges.description: A model API meets its accuracy target but sometimes takes several seconds to respond. What should deployment monitoring include?

choices.text: Prediction latency, alongside relevant model and input-quality measures.
Only the training accuracy saved before deployment.
Only the number of source-code comments.
The final test labels on every API request.

challenges.hint: Production quality includes service behavior as well as model scores.

solution.code: Prediction latency, alongside relevant model and input-quality measures.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: An API can be operationally poor even if its offline accuracy is strong.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Monitoring response latency helps detect service problems that offline evaluation does not capture.

challenges.title: Detecting Invalid Production Inputs
challenges.description: A deployed model starts receiving missing values in a field that was always present during training. What should the team monitor?

choices.text: Only the model title displayed in the dashboard.
Input quality and missingness at inference time.
The training loss as a substitute for checking requests.
Future labels before they become available.

challenges.hint: Compare incoming data with the assumptions made during training.

solution.code: Input quality and missingness at inference time.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Missing fields can change or prevent model predictions.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Input-quality checks can detect a shift or data-contract failure early.

challenges.title: Choosing an Inference Mode
challenges.description: A business needs to score one nightly file containing millions of records, and immediate per-record responses are unnecessary. Which deployment pattern is a natural fit?

choices.text: A synchronous API request for every record with no batching.
A manual edit of each predicted label.
A batch job that scores the file on a schedule.
A model-training run that uses the file as future test labels.

challenges.hint: Match the serving pattern to the timing and volume requirement.

solution.code: A batch job that scores the file on a schedule.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The task is a large scheduled workload rather than an interactive request.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Batch inference can process the file together without requiring immediate responses.

challenges.title: Behavior Changes After Launch
challenges.description: A model is monitored after launch, and the mix of user requests gradually shifts away from the training data. What should the team do?

choices.text: Compare incoming data and production performance with the assumptions and evaluation data used before launch.
Assume the original test score guarantees the same performance indefinitely.
Stop monitoring because the model artifact has not changed.
Use future production labels as inputs to current predictions.

challenges.hint: Production inputs can change even when the deployed model stays fixed.

solution.code: Compare incoming data and production performance with the assumptions and evaluation data used before launch.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The distribution of requests has moved away from the data used in offline evaluation.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Monitor the shift and resulting performance; a fixed test score cannot guarantee quality for changing behavior.

challenges.title: Why Record a Model Version
challenges.description: A production incident occurs, and the team needs to identify exactly which trained model served a request. What capability helps?

choices.text: Reusing one unlabelled model file that is overwritten at every release.
Versioning the deployed model and recording the version used.
Removing deployment records after each request.
Changing evaluation labels until the incident disappears.

challenges.hint: Think about how to trace a prediction back to a specific release.

solution.code: Versioning the deployed model and recording the version used.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Without a stable version identifier, it is hard to know which artifact produced an output.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Versioned deployment records support diagnosis and controlled release management.

challenges.title: Validate Data During Ingestion
challenges.description: A daily source file sometimes omits a required target field. At what stage should a data pipeline detect this?

choices.text: Only after a model has been deployed for several weeks.
By silently creating random target values during prediction.
After computing final test accuracy and deleting the source file.
During data validation before downstream training uses the file.

challenges.hint: Place the check as close as possible to the incoming data.

solution.code: During data validation before downstream training uses the file.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The missing field is detectable when the file enters the pipeline.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Early validation prevents malformed data from flowing into transformations or training.

challenges.title: Ordering Data Pipeline Stages
challenges.description: Which sequence best describes a basic model data pipeline?

choices.text: Ingest data, validate it, transform it, then generate features.
Generate features, delete the source, then decide whether data was valid.
Train and deploy first, then ingest data for evaluation.
Inspect final predictions before defining any input schema.

challenges.hint: Follow data from arrival toward model-ready inputs.

solution.code: Ingest data, validate it, transform it, then generate features.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A pipeline begins with source data and checks whether it is usable.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Transformations and feature generation follow ingestion and validation.

challenges.title: Reproducing a Training Dataset
challenges.description: A team needs to rerun an experiment and understand how raw records became model features. What should its pipeline preserve?

choices.text: Only the final model accuracy rounded to a whole number.
The defined transformation and feature-generation steps used for that run.
A different undocumented transformation for each rerun.
The final test labels embedded in the training features.

challenges.hint: Ask what would let another run repeat the same data preparation.

solution.code: The defined transformation and feature-generation steps used for that run.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: Raw data alone does not describe the transformations applied to it.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Preserving pipeline logic and relevant run inputs makes feature generation more reproducible.

challenges.title: A Source Column Changes Type
challenges.description: A data provider changes an amount field from numeric values to text strings. What should a robust pipeline do?

choices.text: Silently treat every string as a valid numeric amount.
Replace all model predictions with the new source values.
Detect the schema or type change and stop or flag invalid processing.
Skip validation because data types cannot affect features.

challenges.hint: Consider how a change at the source affects later transformations.

solution.code: Detect the schema or type change and stop or flag invalid processing.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A type change can break or alter numeric feature calculations.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Schema validation can catch the problem before corrupted features reach training or inference.

challenges.title: Detecting a Stale Data Feed
challenges.description: A daily pipeline reports success but processes yesterday's file because today's source feed did not arrive. What check would best catch this?

choices.text: Increase the model's number of layers.
Replace missing records with predictions from the final test set.
Validate that the incoming data is fresh and corresponds to the expected run date.
Disable ingestion so every run uses the oldest available file.

challenges.hint: Check whether the pipeline processed the data expected for this run.

solution.code: Validate that the incoming data is fresh and corresponds to the expected run date.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: A pipeline can execute without errors while still using stale inputs.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A freshness or expected-date check can flag the missing feed before downstream transformations and training.

challenges.title: One Prediction Versus Overall Behavior
challenges.description: An analyst wants to explain why one specific loan application received a high risk score. Which explanation view is most relevant?

choices.text: A global ranking that summarizes model behavior across all applications only.
A time-series forecast of next month's loan volume.
A training metric that does not examine this application.
A local explanation for that individual prediction.

challenges.hint: Match the scope of the explanation to the question being asked.

solution.code: A local explanation for that individual prediction.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: The question concerns one application's prediction.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A local attribution examines which inputs contributed to that particular model output.

challenges.title: Summarizing Model Behavior
challenges.description: A team wants to understand which features the model relies on most across a large evaluation set. Which analysis is most suitable?

choices.text: A local explanation for only one randomly chosen prediction.
A global feature-importance summary across the set.
A final test label used as a model input.
A deployment latency measurement.

challenges.hint: Choose a view that aggregates behavior across many examples.

solution.code: A global feature-importance summary across the set.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: One prediction cannot represent how a model behaves on a broad dataset.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: A global summary describes patterns of feature importance across the evaluated examples.

challenges.title: Using an Explanation to Debug
challenges.description: An explanation for a single prediction shows that a strange placeholder field has a large contribution. What is a useful next action?

choices.text: Inspect the input and pipeline to see why that field influenced the prediction.
Conclude immediately that the placeholder causes the real-world outcome.
Assume the model is accurate for every subgroup.
Change the target label to match the explanation.

challenges.hint: Use the explanation as a clue to investigate model behavior.

solution.code: Inspect the input and pipeline to see why that field influenced the prediction.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: An unusual contribution may indicate an unexpected input or learned reliance.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Checking the record and feature pipeline can help identify a data or modeling issue without treating attribution as causal proof.

challenges.title: Interpreting Attribution Carefully
challenges.description: Two explanation methods give different feature attributions for the same prediction. What is a careful response?

choices.text: Average the two explanations and treat the result as ground truth.
Assume one method proves which feature caused the outcome.
Review each method's assumptions and use a suitable method for the question.
Ignore the model output and report whichever explanation is simpler.

challenges.hint: Explanations are produced by methods with their own assumptions.

solution.code: Review each method's assumptions and use a suitable method for the question.

steps.title: Interpret the evidence
steps.explanation: An attribution is not a direct observation of causality.

steps.title: Apply the concept
steps.explanation: Comparing assumptions and validating a suitable explanation prevents overclaiming what the model explanation establishes.

challenges.title: Architecture for images
challenges.description: Which architecture is commonly used to learn local spatial patterns in images through convolutional filters?

choices.text: A convolutional neural network (CNN).
A plain lookup table with no learned parameters.
A rule that sorts images by filename.
A histogram of target labels.

challenges.hint: Look for filters applied across spatial locations.
